This research examines a distributed regulation issue where a parabolic equation with random initial data serves as the target system to control. By leveraging a weak formulation and a mixed finite element method, we obtain a numerical scheme to approximate the solution of this control problem. The existence and a uniform bound for the succession of the discrete solutions are established. Furthermore, we prove that the sequence of the solutions converges to the solution of the continuous control problem as the mesh size approaches zero. The findings are validated by a computational experiment using a Gaussian random field as the initial condition. The results indicate that the numerical dissipation has a noticeable impact on the spatial extent of the affected area and the time it takes for the solution to reach a steady state, but it has little effect on the mean and standard deviation of the solution. The application of the numerical scheme to a two-dimensional case with random initial data is also demonstrated. The code used for the simulations is written in Python 3.8 and the Larch-MPI framework is utilized for parallel computations. The simulations were carried out on a Linux-based cluster with up to 128 processors and yielded satisfactory scalability. The numerical solutions were compared to the analytical solutions obtained using the Kirchhoff approximation and the differences were found to be acceptable. The study highlights the importance of incorporating numerical dissipation to prevent oscillations in the solutions and the impact of different finite element approximations methods on the solutions. The results also demonstrate that the scheme can be efficiently applied to large-scale problems. The code and simulation data are available online. Tables with functional dependencies have been utilized in research to address data integration challenges. In this paper, we define a type of hypergraph that represents tables incorporating functional dependencies and missing values. We then propose a method for identifying isomorphic hypergraphs, which are essential for comparing and merging data tables. We also develop a process for determining if two hypergraphs are joinable, achieving the goal of data integration. Additionally, we provide a characterization of joinable hypergraphs that can be achieved through a sequence of successive extension operations. These results form the foundation for further exploration into data exchange, querying, and materialization, as well as views and self-joinability, all within the context of tables that incorporate null values and functional dependencies. Notably, our approach differs from existing methods that rely on elimination rules due to its utilization of extension operations. We demonstrate the superiority of our approach by showing that existing methods that utilize elimination rules can be replicated using the proposed method of extension operations, yet the converse is not true. We also provide an alternate, more efficient algorithm for determining self-joinability compared to existing methods. We conclude by highlighting the broad implications of our results, which can be applied to various data management tasks and provide a platform for exploring additional research questions. We use graph theory and hypergraph theory to formally define and analyze the proposed hypergraph tables, which enables us to generalize and expand on existing research presented in the data exchange and relational theory literature. We show that our definition of joinable hypergraphs is equivalent to the existing concept of self-joinability, which in turn is equivalent to the concept of data consistency introduced by Fagin. We also explore the relationship between extension operations and elimination rules, which leads to a characterization of joinable hypergraphs based on the presence or absence of specific paths. We end by highlighting the limitations of our approach and identifying potential future research directions. We believe that our results and approach can be applied to various data management tasks and provide a platform for exploring additional research questions. Time series data exhibiting periodic counts pose significant challenges due to their intricate cyclic nature, lack of synchrony, and varying length, which complicates modeling and forecasting tasks. To address these difficulties, we develop a novel Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregressive model, TVPAR, that effectively captures the periodic characteristics and statistical relationships within these datasets. Unlike existing periodic models that assume perfect periodicity and joint renewal process models that are asymptotic in nature, our proposed TVPAR model takes into account irregularities in data duration and employs a data-driven approach to forecast future periods. We establish the consistency of the maximum likelihood estimator for TVPAR and utilize this proof to show that the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true and estimated data-generating distributions converges as the sample size increases. Furthermore, we derive a $\sqrt{h}$-asymptotic expansion for the difference between the log-likelihood function evaluated at the true and estimated parameters, which enables us to obtain the asymptotic distribution of the plug-in TVPAR estimator and forecast evaluation criteria. We leverage a shooting method to numerically solve the optimal change-point problem and implement a Monte Carlo simulation study as well as real-world applications to demonstrate the performance and efficacy of TVPAR. The R software package for TVPAR is available upon request. Creating accurate models for robot manipulation requires developing reliable object representation methods that account for pose, shape, and other relevant attributes. In order to achieve successful manipulation tasks, representations must be able to distinguish between different object appearances and incorporate essential features such as orientation, position, and surface details. In this research, we introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel framework for generating object representations that incorporate both internal and external attributes. NDFs comprise of two main components: a neural network that generates spatial descriptors and another that defines a distance metric. Both components are trained simultaneously to minimize a contrastive loss function, resulting in a representation that accurately captures both external and internal object properties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NDFs in distinguishing between identical objects with different orientations and those that are identical but with varying shapes and sizes. Furthermore, we show that representations generated using NDFs can be utilized in a learning-based grasping module, leading to a significant improvement in grasping success rates. Experimental results indicate a 27% improvement in grasping success rates when using NDFs in comparison to a baseline method. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub. The novel descriptor field framework presented in this research offers a versatile platform for future extensions and integrations with other learning-based modules. The approach has been specifically designed for applications in manipulation and mobility but has the potential to be utilized in a wide range of computer vision tasks. To analyze the Yang-Lee edge singularity in a wide range of statistical models, the universality of this singularity's features is tested within various O(N) universality classes. By examining the Z2 symmetry breaking associated with the Yang-L Lee edge, we can determine the location where this singularity occurs in each universality class. By calculating the position of this singularity for a specific universality class relative to the ground state or disordered state, we can determine θc = π/N for N ≥ 2. Additionally, we calculate the critical exponent ν in relation to N, finding ν = (N/2)(ν0 - 1) with ν0 ≈ 1.37. These calculations are performed within the mean-field approximation, but yield results that are independent of this approximation. In fact, our analysis shows that the edge singularity's position and associated critical exponents are determined solely by the symmetry of the underlying universality class, rather than any specific microscopic details. As a result, we find that the edge singularity's position and associated critical exponents are the same for the Ising model in 4-Euclidean dimensions and N = 1 dimensional Ising models. Similarly, we also find that the edge singularity's position and associated critical exponents are the same for the 3D Ising model and N = 3 dimensional O(3) scalar theories. These findings are significant because they indicate that the edge singularity's position and associated critical exponents are non-trivial, rather than being determined by any mean-field approximation. As a further consequence, we also find that the Asymptotic High-Temperature Series cannot be used to determine the edge singularity's position and associated critical exponents. As a replacement, we recommend using a Cumulant Expansion approach. As an illustration of this recommendation, we provide an estimate of the edge singularity's position for the Z2 symmetry breaking associated with the Yang-L Lee edge in 4-Euclidean dimensions, finding θc ≈ 1.44045. As a broader application of this approach, we also provide an estimate of the edge singularity's position for the Z2 symmetry breaking associated with the Yang-L Lee edge in N = 1 dimensional Ising models, finding θc ≈ 1.44045. As a final consequence, we also find that the edge singularity's position and associated critical exponents are the same for the 3D Ising model and N = 3 dimensional O(3) scalar theories

Reconstructing 3D scenes relying on images taken from known viewpoints has seen significant advancements in recent years. Despite these breakthroughs, estimating the 6D pose of a novel object from a single image has proven to be a more elusive goal. In response to this challenge, researchers have turned to images of the object taken from various angles, yet this approach is often limited by the availability and quality of such data. This paper addresses this constraint by presenting the DeepHMap++ architecture, capable of estimating the 6D pose of an object from a single image without relying on training images of the object itself. DeepHMap++ leverages a projection group loss and correspondence learning to achieve this goal, successfully applying it to objects with limited training data. When comparing DeepHMap++ to other state-of-the-art methods using the CPM dataset, it demonstrates improved performance, and on the LVIS dataset, it shows comparable results while utilizing a significantly smaller dataset. Furthermore, we showcase the generalization of DeepHMap++ to estimate the 6D pose of novel objects from single images, without prior knowledge of their 3D models. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub.

estimates a distribution's underlying graph structure while accounting for
covariate influences, offering a generalization of traditional Graphical Lasso
methods. The GGLasso package offers a range of capabilities, including
estimation, cross-validation, and precision matrix spectral penalty selection
tools. It also provides a GUI for user-adjustable hyperparameter selection

analysis" published in the journal BMC Bioinformatics. The package's name is
an acronym for Generalized Graphical Lasso, and the source code is available
at https://github.com/kuanghou/GGLasso. The package's documentation is located
at http://kuanghou.github.io/GGLasso/. The package can be installed using pip

Numerous biomolecular simulations rely on precise sampling of configurational space to accurately describe molecular behavior, often involving complex motions and rapid changes. Despite its efficiency, the applicability of Langevin dynamics is limited for force-field simulations in the past due to computational constraints, though it has found uses in various methods, such as reweighting and biased simulations. Here, we outline the implementation of a high-performance algorithm using Langevin dynamics for biased simulations and discuss the implications of our findings within this context. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in producing biased samples and assess its scope for further development in conjunction with other techniques, such as thermostatting methods and enhanced sampling algorithms. The code used in this study has been made publicly available as a module within the GROMACS molecular simulation package. By leveraging our approach, researchers can harness the analytical advantages of Langevin dynamics to enhance the efficacy of their biomolecular simulations. The current implementation can be found online at: https://github.com/gromacs/gromacs/tree/master/src/ModuleMDLBiasLangevinDynamics.

Recently, researchers have focused on the methods to analyze prominent eigenvectors in single-layer networks. However, a natural extension to this technique has not been established for multilayer networks. Here, we develop a general approach to identify the most distinctive eigenvectors across all connected layers. We then create a combination method that integrates the significant values of each eigenvector in each layer to determine a unified measure of prominence for multilayer networks. Additionally, we explore a weighted average approach to combine the eigenvectors across all layers to derive a collective eigenvector. Both the integrated and weighted average methods facilitate the identification of standout nodes that exhibit distinct community affiliations or characteristics. We validate these methods using simulated data sets and real-world examples, including a notable case involving a multilayer sports network. Both the integrated and weighted average approaches yield comparable results and accurately pinpoint the most prominent nodes across all layers. We also examine the relationship between the node-significance layer density and eigenvector prominence and find that the most prominent nodes often lie at the intersection of nodes with high or intermediate-significance across all layers. We term this phenomenon "prominence parity". We hypothesize that the presence of nodes with high-significance in one layer may diminish the prominence of corresponding nodes in another layer, depending on the connectedness between the two layers. We test and validate this hypothesis using a simulated data set and real-world multilayer networks and propose several potential applications to showcase the versatility of the eigenvector prominence method for multilayer networks. We also explore the relationship between the collective eigenvector and node-community affiliation or characteristic and find that the most prominent nodes often exhibit distinct community affiliations or characteristics. We term this phenomenon "community centrality" and hypothesize that the most prominent nodes often lie at the intersection of high community centrality and low node-significance across all layers. We test and validate this hypothesis using real-world multilayer networks and propose several potential applications to showcase the versatility of the eigenvector prominence method for multilayer networks. We conclude by discussing the theoretical underpinnings of the eigenvector prominence method for multilayer networks, propose several potential directions for future research, and provide software for reproducibility purposes. We hope that this research will pave the way for further advancements in network analysis and inspire future applications of the eigenvector prominence method for multilayer networks. We also hope that this research will contribute to the development of more robust and universal measures of node-prominence in multilayer networks

This study investigates how spheres interact with a liquid surface at moderate speeds, a previously unexplored area for this type of seal research. To understand and describe the behavior of spheres in this speed range, new mathematical models are developed to capture the key features observed during impact and subsequent movement across the liquid surface. Comparisons with existing models and new numerical simulations are conducted to map the spheres' motion and identify different regimes of behavior based on speed and surface tension. The development of these models provides insights that could be applied to real-world problems, such as reducing splashes in liquid-based systems that incorporate moving spheres. The research also delves into the specifics of spheres that bounce, stick, or create large splashes, offering a framework for classifying the different outcomes of high-speed impacts. The models and associated analysis can be adapted to other curved surfaces and may offer a starting point for related studies on the interaction between moving objects and liquid surfaces. The research is further supported by and builds upon the findings of a related previous study on the motion of spheres below the threshold of splashing. Cupricite CuFe2S3 is an unusual mineral exhibiting both strong covalent bonding in iron oxide anion clusters and significant electron correlation in copper ions. X-ray absorption fine structure measurements reveal the presence of localized, low-spin 3d (S=0) states in the copper and, with the aid of theoretical calculations, detailed orbital characteristics. Theoretical modeling also provides insight into the band formation within the iron oxide anion clusters, classifying them as Mott-Hubbans type. Unique anion cluster orbital filling is suggested by the presence of an anisotropic magnetic moment and is supported by calculations of the magnetic moments from both theoretical and experimental perspectives. Uncommon orbital selection and localization in cupricite are attributed to the unique balance of electron interaction, anisotropic crystal field effects, and strong covalency among the cupricite ions. This rare balance results in an anisotropic magnetic moment, an exceptional mineralological occurrence of an Mott-Hubbard cluster in an anisotropic arrangement, making cupricite an exciting subject for further interdisciplinary study. Quasi-one-dimensional turbostratic graphene, with its irregular herringbone arrangement, presents a unique situation where the external magnetic field component parallel to the layer can be neglected due to its extremely small value. By leveraging this distinctive feature, we investigate excitons in this material and develop a theoretical framework to predict their behavior under an external electric field. Our model reveals the existence of obscure excitons and predicts a distinctive "hidden" state characterized by massive amplitude oscillations when subjected to a specific critical intensity of electric field. This predicted behavior has been verified through numerical simulations and can potentially be experimentally confirmed using time-resolved spectroscopy. Notably, our findings suggest that even without an external magnetic field, the spatial distribution of excitons can exhibit enormous Rabi-like oscillations, a discovery that expands the scope of this phenomenon beyond curved and magnetic field-induced situations. By exploring the influence of an external electric field on the hidden state, we identify potential for controlling and confirming the predicted massive amplitude oscillations, thereby providing a feasible pathway to experimentally verify our results. Our theoretical framework also offers a practical means for calculating the energy of obscure excitons in any two-dimensional system with broken rotational symmetry. By further extending our model to account for interactions between excitons, we demonstrate that the hidden state can serve as a precursor to exciton-dressing and that the observed huge Rabi-like oscillations can be attributed to the internal angular momentum of the exciton. This interpretation is also supported by the calculated energy of the exciton-dressing state and is in agreement with earlier research on curved and magnetic field-induced situations. Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states have a specific property where the presence of a photon triggers the generation of a given coherent state. These states hold significant potential for use in quantum metrology and communication systems. Initially, it seemed impossible to create these states using only a single parameter, but research has demonstrated that they can be generated through quantum-optical catalysis with the aid of a beam splitter and a coherent state serving as a catalyst. By replacing the beam splitter with a Mach-Zehnder interferometer equipped with a phase modulator, it's now possible to produce these states using a single parameter. Furthermore, this setup enables continuous variation of the states' complexity by adjusting a key parameter. Additionally, both catalytic and non-catalytic versions of these states exhibit identical physical characteristics, allowing them to be interconverted through a process known as "quantum state rearrangement". These findings pave the way for implementing single-photon facilitated coherent states within various quantum systems. Moreover, an experimental setup that can generate these states has been proposed, offering the potential to expand the range of available quantum states in optomechanical systems. Lastly, we outline a strategy for converting these states back to their original form following a measurement, and discuss the implications for related coherent states.

Code-mixing occurs when an individual switches between two or more languages within a sentence, a common phenomenon observed in areas where multiple languages coexist and speakers possess a high level of proficiency in two languages. This practice is particularly prevalent among bilingual individuals who have a strong grasp of two languages, often incorporating code-mixing in spoken and written communication. Present research views code-mixing as an indicator of a speaker's advanced linguistic abilities, resulting from the interplay between their two languages and influenced by factors such as cognitive, social, and linguistic in nature. Despite its prevalence, code-mixing remains underrepresented in language studies, and current code-mixing analysis is largely qualitative in nature. This paper delves into the backgrounds of code-mixing, explores existing research on the topic, discusses various factors contributing to code-mixing, and examines its implications for NLP applications. We also discuss the challenges and opportunities in developing code-mixing NLP models and highlight the need for more systematic and quantitative studies on code-mixing. Finally, we outline potential future research directions in code-mixing NLP, emphasizing the significance of incorporating code-mixing data for model pretraining and evaluating multilingual language models. By exploring these research avenues, we aim to advance our understanding of code-mixing and its impact on linguistic theory, and to create more effective NLP models capable of handling real-world language data. We hope this work will also serve as a foundation for further studies on code-mixing in other areas and communities. Tantalum oxide, Ta$_2$O$_5$, is a highly intriguing material whose crystal structure is difficult to determine due to the presence of multiple polymorphs and stabilization of the oxide anion in a 5+ state. As a result, there is ongoing debate about the Ta$_2$O$_5$ ground state structure. Previous studies have identified three stable structures, namely the columbite, schelienite, and tantalite structures, with the columbite structure being the most stable by about 0.3 eV per formula unit when compared to the other two. Using Monte Carlo simulations in combination with DFT calculations, researchers found that the Ta$_2$O$_5$ crystal structure can exhibit a first-order phase transition at temperatures above 800K, ultimately stabilizing in the schelienite configuration. Conversely, below this temperature, the columbite structure becomes the most stable state. These findings suggest that the schelienite structure could potentially represent the Ta$_2$O$_5$ ground state in high-temperature conditions. Consequently, further research is necessary to confirm the validity of these results and explore ways to experimentally verify the predicted phase transition. If confirmed, it would provide a rare example of a transition between two crystalline states at temperatures relevant to material synthesis. Experimental techniques such as X-ray diffraction and synchrotron radiation could be used to investigate the predicted phase transition and shed light on the Ta$_2$O$_5$ ground state structure. If the schelienite structure is confirmed as the ground state, it would have significant implications for materials synthesis and device fabrication due to the differing properties exhibited by the columbite and schelienite structures. For instance, research has shown that the schelienite structure exhibits improved piezoelectric and ferroelectric properties when compared to the columbite structure. If the Ta$_2$O$_5$ ground state structure is found to be the schelienite configuration, it would also provide a rare example of how the arrangement of atoms within a material can be controlled through temperature alone. If the columbite structure is confirmed as the ground state instead, it would require a reevaluation of the theoretical models used to predict its properties. The Big Geographic Sort refers to the self-reinforcing pattern of urban residents moving away from cities and relocating to suburban areas, while rural areas remain populated by long-standing local residents. This research investigates the relationship between this phenomenon and the spread of misinformation on Reddit. By examining posts across various platforms and identifying false information about COVID-19 vaccines, we discovered a correlation between users located in urban areas and those who shared conspiracy theories. Furthermore, we found that users in suburban areas were more likely to engage with dubious information than their urban counterparts. However, we also discovered that the likelihood of users in suburban areas accepting this information as true was greater than those in urban areas. Additionally, we observed that users in rural areas were more inclined to believe this information than those in both urban and suburban areas. By incorporating elements of social influence and considering the varying levels of connection among users in different geographic locations, we were able to interpret these findings. Notably, we discovered that users in urban areas who were connected to a smaller number of other users were more susceptible to spreading misinformation, whereas those connected to a larger number of users were less likely to do so. On the other hand, the prevalence of misinformation in rural areas can be attributed to the closed social system prevalent in these areas, which hinders the influence of external information and fosters greater adherence to previously held beliefs. Ultimately, our analysis provides a framework for understanding how the Big Geographic Sort may contribute to the dissemination and persistence of misinformation in these communities.

By analyzing the acoustic data resulting from human instructors guiding robots through manipulation tasks, our research aims to identify distinct sound patterns associated with specific robot actions, such as grasping or releasing objects. We developed a method to extract features from the audio signals produced by humans instructing robots and evaluated our approach using a dataset from a manipulation task where a human teaches a robot to pick up objects using different grip types. Our results show that by utilizing features derived from the convolutional neural network architecture, we can accurately classify the underlying robot actions based on the associated audio signals. Conversational interfaces are becoming increasingly popular and have wide-ranging applications, but testing them poses a significant challenge due to the lack of standardized protocols. A well-structured approach to testing conversational systems involves evaluating not only their functionality but also their ability to maintain coherent discussions with users. Existing testing frameworks for conversational systems are generally limited in their ability to simulate complex, real-world user interactions and typically focus solely on assessing individual components of the system rather than testing its overall performance in conversational scenarios. In contrast, we present a testing framework known as Converse, which enables systematic testing of a bot's conversational capabilities across multiple dimensions by simulating various types of user interactions, including both one-to-one text conversations and group dialogues. Converse offers a comprehensive suite of tests that can be executed automatically to evaluate a bot's performance and identify areas for improvement. By utilizing Converse, we were able to rectify several issues with a real-world bot developed for medical applications, demonstrating the utility and effectiveness of our testing framework. The Converse framework is available to the public via an open-source license. In addition to Converse, we developed a command-line tool called converse-run that facilitates easy execution of tests on a bot, allowing for both automated testing of a bot in isolation and integration with testing frameworks like Maven. The tool is also openly available. The Converse framework has been successfully applied in a real-world context, specifically in developing a testing plan for a medical bot discussed in a separate paper titled "A Safety Case for a Medical Bot" presented at the SAFECAM 2020 conference. The testing plan we created comprises 106 test cases that cover critical aspects of the bot's medical knowledge and has been utilized to improve the bot's performance to a satisfactory level for clinical use. The Converse framework has been found to be highly adaptable and has been successfully applied in other, unrelated domains outside of the medical field. The framework's versatility stems from its non-proprietary nature, lack of specific medical domain knowledge, and general applicability to testing conversational systems. The Converse framework has been further enhanced by the inclusion of additional testing features, specifically designed to evaluate a bot's ability to adhere to predetermined conversation protocols, in addition to its existing capabilities in assessing a bot's performance in open-ended conversations. The enhanced Converse framework now comprises over 300 test cases, demonstrating its broad applicability to a wide range of conversational systems and its ability to assess a bot's performance in various types of conversations, including multi-turn dialogues, group conversations

Cross-domain recommendation has been widely used in recent years, especially in multi-sparse-domain scenarios, which have significant applications in E-commerce platforms, although there are limited studies on this topic. Existing multi-sparse-domain cross-recommendation methods typically rely on the assumption that users' preferences can be connected through a unified and consistent structure, which may not always hold true in real-world scenarios. This paper proposes a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation framework, termed MSDCR, which breaks free from the conventional uniform and consistent preference structure paradigm. MSDCR introduces a mixture of distinct domain-specific sparse distributions to capture the complexity of user preferences without imposing unnecessary constraints. This allows for recommending items across domains that have no previous interaction data, which was previously impossible with current multi-sparse-domain cross-recommendation methods. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of MSDCR over state-of-the-art baselines, which were specifically designed to handle uniform preference structures. The accuracy of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is crucial for precise medical diagnosis, and its quality must be consistently checked before using the data. Although artificial neural networks have improved MRI image reconstruction and classification efficiency, their limited data availability hinders their practical application in MRI quality assessment. Available datasets are often restricted, making it difficult to develop models that generalize well to new, unknown situations. This study proposes a novel neural network architecture that effectively detects brain MRI defects in clinical settings, where multiple variables influence image quality and there is limited data available. This model utilizes a low-resolution feature map to improve classification performance and demonstrates superior generalization capabilities in multiple MRI quality assessment scenarios. When evaluating generalization performance, the proposed network achieves comparable results to a model trained on high-quality data, with a 25% improvement in classification accuracy when transferring it to a new dataset with different acquisition parameters. This demonstrates its ability to adapt to new situations with minimal retraining, reducing the need for additional data and facilitating seamless integration into existing MRI workflows. This model has the potential to be a valuable tool for training and optimizing MRI protocols, as well as enhancing image post-processing and reconstruction techniques. The context in which an object appears can significantly influence the outcome of an object recognition algorithm. Although numerous approaches emphasize the importance of considering context, a well-structured framework to evaluate the impact of context for trained object recognition models does not exist. In response to this gap, we propose a context assessment metric that gauges the impact of context on the models' performance and provides a threshold-based strategy to determine whether the context is beneficial or if the model has reached saturation. We demonstrate and analyze this metric's utility using a widely used dataset. By examining the relationship between the proposed metric and existing quality evaluation methods, we also explore how it can be utilized to identify robust object recognition models. In addition, we investigate the relationship between the proposed metric and existing quantity evaluation methods, examining how it can be utilized to determine optimal scene occlusion levels for the models. We make the proposed assessment framework available to the research community. By systematically analyzing the impact of context on trained object recognition models, we provide an empirical study of a wide range of real-world images, uncovering both general and image-specific context effects. We discuss potential applications and future research directions in the paper's conclusion.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face multiple possible responses 
for any given history, leading to an extremely large output space. To manage 
this, we propose a new model that instead picks specific response continuations 
from a limited set, making conversational branching more feasible. We introduce 
the MultiTalk Dataset, a large collection of dialogue data featuring numerous 
branching paths and straightforward continuations. In our experiments, we use 
this dataset to train and evaluate various models, including a baseline that 
merely generates full responses. Our results reveal that models trained on the 
continuation task excel at predicting both immediate and future response 
branchings. Furthermore, when incorporated into a dialogue system, these models
achieve superior performance in a wide-range conversation setting. We make the 
MultiTalk Dataset and associated code publicly available. With its extensive 
branching possibilities, this dataset offers valuable insights and tools for 
developing and evaluating dialogue systems through varied conversational paths.

While participating in a learning process, a user with sensitive data typically does not benefit directly.  They must rely on the learner, who applies the trained model, to provide them with useful information.  We identify a significant vulnerability in such interactions: users with sensitive data are susceptible to deceitful attacks originating from the learner.  We term these assaults "privacy shoves."  We analyze two types of privacy shoves: one that misleads a user into contributing more sensitive data and another that misleads them into contributing more frequently.  We establish conditions under which both kinds of assaults are feasible.  We also determine the optimal assault strategy for both types, which in one case involves distributing more sensitive data and in the other case involves increasing the frequency of data contributions.  We further investigate the impact of these assaults on learning and find that both types result in overfitting.  We propose several possible solutions to counter these assaults, which include incorporating the user's willingness to contribute as additional data, implementing adversarial training to make the model robust, or introducing noise to the user's updates.  We test and evaluate these solutions using synthetic data and find that they are all effective in counteracting the assaults.  We also explore feasible real-world applications where both kinds of privacy shoves could occur and discuss the limitations of our study.  We term these assaults "privacy shoves" to highlight their deceptive nature and emphasize their significance in guiding future research aimed at exploring additional possible solutions.  We believe that investigating these assaults will contribute to the development of more secure and beneficial learning interactions for users with sensitive data.  We propose a research direction that involves developing methods to detect these assaults and encourage future work in this area.  We suggest several possible detection methods and discuss the challenges associated with discovering the optimal solution for both the learner and the user.  We conclude by discussing the implications of these assaults on several real-world applications and suggest ways to prevent them in such contexts. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating and managing safe, efficient transportation systems. Research has focused on analyzing and modeling the spread and stability of networks, often using mathematical and computational methods to evaluate their resilience. In this study, we investigate the percolation dynamics of networks using the basic contact process model. Our main objective is to determine how the distribution of connection degrees affects the spread and stability of networks. To achieve this, we develop a mathematical framework to analyze the transition probabilities of percolation on a Cayley tree model. By applying and modifying the Eden cluster growth model, we can simulate the spread of networks and gather statistics on the distribution of connected components. Our results show that the distribution of connected components follows a power law, with the exact power law index dependent on the network's parameters. We also examine the effects of changing network parameters on the distribution of connected components and find that even small changes can lead to a shift in the distribution from a power law to a log-normal distribution due to a phase transition, causing the networks to become more fragmented. We term and study this phenomenon, known as the "avalanche transition," and find that its characteristics vary depending on the network's parameters. Our research highlights the importance of considering the distribution of connection degrees when evaluating network stability and suggests that phase transitions can occur even in simple networks, affecting their ability to spread information and withstand attacks. We believe that our findings have broader implications for understanding complex networks and can be applied to analyzing and managing real-world transportation systems. A novel, sloshing-Sagnic interferometer configuration is proposed to achieve this goal and improve the frequency range of these detectors to 100 Hz. This proposed design leverages the influence of back-scattered signals causing a phase shift in a liquid's oscillatory state, which can be detected. The proposed system's noise has been simulated, indicating that it can effectively reduce thermal noise below 10 Hz and radiation noise below 100 Hz, making it an attractive option for next-generation gravitational wave detectors. With optimization, this design could potentially reduce radiation noise below 50 Hz, an achievement that would require further advancements in materials to reduce thermal noise to levels comparable to other noise sources. The proposed system's performance can be benchmarked against a conventional Big Bird resonant recycling interferometer design, demonstrating that the sloshing-Sagnic design can offer improved performance in a wider frequency range. The development of this design also offers the benefit of being compatible with existing gravitational wave detector infrastructure. The proposed system's noise characteristics can be improved by utilizing a different liquid with reduced thermal noise, a concept that has been tested using a realistic simulation of the Advanced LIGO+ parameter space. The thermal noise of various liquids has been calculated and compared to the proposed system's noise, demonstrating that it is possible to minimize this noise to frequencies as low as 20 Hz with optimal liquid selection. The development of the sloshing-Sagnic design has also been compared to other proposed gravitational wave detector designs, including a variant of the LIGO+ recycling resonant interferometer and a design that incorporates a sapphire end mirror, both of which have shown comparable performance in noise simulations. Recently, Extensive Line-Of-Sight (XLOS) models have gained popularity in modeling the visibility of Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) systems. Although these models capture the visibility statistics accurately, their computational simplicity comes at the cost of complex non-linear equations describing the visibility regions' boundaries. As a result, finding the exact points where the visibility regions of different base stations intersect has been found to be computationally challenging. To overcome this limitation, this paper re-examines the condition for non-intersecting visibility areas in XLOS models and provides a more straightforward and linearly expressed condition. Furthermore, this research extends the previous findings by considering the random locations of small cells within a large cell and derives an analytical expression for the probability of non-intersecting visibility areas. To validate the proposed model, an extensive simulation is conducted, and the results are compared with existing empirical data. Additionally, this paper explores various small-cell deployment configurations and provides precise, linearly-defined probabilities for the specified scenarios. These results can be beneficial for system designers and engineers in assessing and analyzing the spatial coverage and visibility areas in large-scale MIMO systems.

In young stellar systems, continuum substructures in protoplanetary disks are commonly observed, and a leading explanation attributes their formation to vertical shear instability (VSI). As a follow-up to a previous computational study, this work develops empirical predictions for a model that incorporates the statistical properties of substructures seen in VSI-driven disks. Using a radiative transfer simulation tool, we examine the emission patterns of Tdisk models with varying inclination angles, radiative transfer models, and spectral filters to mimic observations at multiple wavelengths. Comparing the results to observed continuum profiles, we find that the presence of VSI can mimic the features of other phenomena, such as disk asymmetry, gaps, and exoplanet influence. However, its distinctive effect is limited to a specific wavelength range, where the peak brightness of the inner disk is 10-20% greater than usual. Notably, VSI's impact is largely unaffected by the presence of an embedded planet or a disk with an inner hole. By correlating the spatial distribution of substructures with specific wavelengths, we can potentially identify the underlying physical processes shaping the disk. As such, this study highlights the value of multi-wavelength observations in probing the vertical structure of protoplanetary disks. In the absence of true 3D radiative transfer simulations, our models based on 2D projections offer a practical, observable signature of VSI-driven substructures that can be verified through future observations with higher sensitivity and multi-wavelength capabilities.

Neural language models have largely surpassed $n$-gram models due to better performance, however, their increased complexity hinders their ability to quickly adapt to new data. In contrast, $n$-gram models excel at fast incorporation of new information but are eclipsed by neural models in accuracy. We explore a novel approach where a neural model serves as a teacher to augment the features of $n$-gram models by generating residual attributes that $n$-gram models find difficult to capture on their own. We employ this setup in a task where a neural model is trained to create text based on input prompts but falls short due to limited data. We find that this method successfully leverages the strengths of both models, resulting in created text that is more sophisticated and coherent according to human evaluators and automated metrics. Moreover, the generated residuals play a crucial role in enhancing the features of $n$-gram models as we verify through manipulation of the model architecture. This approach can be applied broadly to tasks involving neural text creation, classification, and masked language modeling. We refer to this approach as the Residual Neural Text Creation ($RNTC$) framework. In our experiments using the $RNTC$ framework on text creation tasks, the inclusion of residual attributes significantly boosts the performance of $n$-gram models, resulting in PER scores of 56.67 for the language modeling task and F1 scores of 80.19 for the text classification task. In addition to text creation, we demonstrate the versatility of the $RNTC$ framework by integrating it into a state-of-the-art BERT-based pretraining regime, known as BERT base, which yields a 5.6\% improvement in the SAT score and a 3.4\% improvement in the ACC score on full and truncated versions respectively. We make the code available at \url{https://github.com/ghr-github/RNTC}.

In this work, we investigate the possibility of forming primordial black holes (PBHs) through the disruption of cosmological perturbations during inflation within a specific class of $\alpha$-attractor models. To accomplish this, we first establish a requirement for effective PBH formation, which is that the amplitude of an scalar perturbation must surpass a particular threshold in comparison to its surrounding area. We then examine this scenario in two distinct contexts: when a particular scalar perturbation falls within the horizon during the late stages of inflation and when it occurs during an inflationary stage with constant slow-roll inflation. We calculate the minimum perturbation necessary to meet our PBH formation criterion and compare it to the natural fluctuations of the scalar perturbations in the early universe. Our analysis indicates that forming PBHs of $M_{\rm PBH} \simeq 10^{10}$ M$_{\odot}$ within these inflationary models might be challenging, but it is feasible for PBHs of $M_{\rm PBH} \simeq 10^{3}$ M$_{\odot}$. Moreover, we find that an appropriate choice of the initial conditions can lead to a distribution of PBH masses, which could potentially align with the masses of compact objects discovered through gravitational waves. We also examine the possibility of forming PBHs in an inflationary stage with a transition from a phase with slow-roll inflation to one with an end, which we refer to as an "inflationary brane." In this scenario, we determine the minimum perturbation required for PBH formation and find that it is significantly larger than the natural fluctuations of the scalar perturbations in the early universe, which might result in PBHs having masses greater than $M_{\rm PBH} \simeq 10^{3}$ M$_{\odot}$. In recent years, significant progress has been made in modeling sequential data with temporal linear models that incorporate current and past observations. These models have been successfully applied to tasks such as user recommendation systems and stock price prediction. We investigate the temporal linear model with the most basic form, which includes the current and all previous observations, and explore its ability to generalize beyond the training data. We provide a theoretical analysis of this model's ability to avoid overfitting when the number of parameters exceeds the sample size. We also compare this model to an alternative, less sequential version and demonstrate its superior performance in certain situations. Furthermore, we offer a practical regularization strategy that takes into account the importance of each observation in the sequence. Finally, we illustrate the model's effectiveness in two real-world applications using synthetic data. We make the code available online for reproducibility purposes.

This research also explores the potential benefits of centralized storage planning control as well as alternative, less expensive cautious self-planning strategies that can help mitigate negative effects without sacrificing market stability. Our study's results can be applied to various market structures and different storage technologies, offering valuable insights for policymakers seeking to design effective, fair, and economically efficient decentralized energy markets. Deep neural networks have consistently excelled at various computer vision tasks, thanks in large part to the vast amount of images used to train them. In this study, a novel method called Dynamic Learning at the ImageNet Scale (DINAS) is proposed to efficiently train high-performing models on relatively small datasets that are derived from a large dataset similar to ImageNet. By leveraging a subset of 2.5 million images from the full ImageNet dataset as a pseudo-supervised source, DINAS develops a unique strategy that achieves comparable performance to training models on large datasets, at a fraction of the required data. When applied to several benchmark datasets, DINAS demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional training methods, with a notable improvement in scaling to larger models. Moreover, an intriguing finding reveals that, with optimal hyperparameter selection, DINAS can even surpass the performance of models trained on full ImageNet, highlighting the vast potential of this method for unlocking the true capabilities of large models on relatively small datasets. By collectively incorporating dynamic learning, pseudo-supervised training, and layer-wise optimization, DINAS offers a versatile framework that can be seamlessly integrated into existing scalable training systems, paving the way for a breakthrough in training high-performing models on modest datasets derived from massive sources. With its versatility, DINAS is suitable for a wide range of applications, from efficient model fine-tuning on medium-sized datasets to the challenging task of training models on minimal datasets comprised of a few thousand images. With minimal modifications, DINAS can be applied to other large-scale classification problems similar to Cifar-100, where it achieves notable performance gains. By leveraging the vast amount of freely available image data on the internet, future work plans to explore ways to further enhance DINAS by incorporating semi-supervised learning, with the ultimate goal of training models on just a single image. With its boundless potential for generalization, DINAS is poised to revolutionize the field of computer vision by unlocking the limitless potential of massive sources of data. Researchers who utilize silicon-based donors for quantum computing are concerned about the potential for nearby silicon defects to influence performance. Specifically, the effect of the silicon divacancy needs to be understood as it is highly prevalent and difficult to eradicate. This study utilizes a multi-valley effective mass approach and accurate CI methods to examine the impact of a nearby donor on a silicon divacancy and simulate various scenarios to better comprehend this interaction's subtleties. By exploring different spin configurations, it becomes evident that the influence of the silicon divacancy is challenging to eliminate, with some scenarios revealing persistent signatures for an indefinitely prolonged period, despite extensive purification efforts. These findings underscore the inevitability of trapped silicon-based donors being affected by silicon divacancies due to the inevitable presence of nearby divacancies, with estimates suggesting that at least one divacancy will influence a donor within a 5 nanometer radius unless excessive ion beam treatment is applied. This research highlights the necessity of developing strategies to either remove silicon divacancies or develop methods to accurately detect them. Additionally, as purification techniques are currently insufficient, the study provides a basis for further investigation into the following crucial issues: divacancy removal, precise divacancy detection, and the development of appropriate quantum error correction protocols. This will be crucial for scaling up silicon-based quantum computing to a 1 millimeter diameter range.

Learners encounter numerous words with multiple senses during language acquisition, posing a significant challenge that persists even after acquiring native language status. Prior research has used a dual-route model to explain how native and non-native language knowledge are processed, yet it generally focuses on semantic processing while overlooking pragmatics. The present study examines the role of context-gloss enhancements in facilitating word sense discrimination (WSD) through a production experiment, considering both semantic and pragmatic contexts. The results indicate that both semantic and pragmatic context-gloss enhancements promote WSD, but the effect of semantic context-gloss enhancement is more pronounced when the target word has a clear context. Conversely, the effect of pragmatic context-gloss enhancement is more noticeable when the target word has an ambiguous context. The study also reveals an interesting finding that context-gloss enhancements exert a positive influence on WSD when the target word is presented in an active rather than a passive sentence role. The observed outcomes are interpreted within the dual-route model framework, suggesting that both semantic and pragmatic context-gloss enhancements facilitate re-activation of the stored word senses in the lexicon, thereby enhancing WSD. The study's findings are expected to contribute to the development of effective pedagogical materials for enhancing L2 WSD capabilities. Additionally, the research provides implications for the dual-route model, proposing that both semantic and pragmatic context-gloss enhancements trigger re-activation of the stored word senses in the lexicon, and offering a possible explanation for the previously observed positive effect of active sentence construction on WSD. The study's results are also expected to benefit the design of computer-assisted language learning systems aimed at enhancing L2 WSD capabilities through context-gloss enhancement. The research's limitations are acknowledged, along with suggestions for future studies on the topic. The study's findings are expected to benefit fields like language acquisition, linguistics, and education. Thanks to advances in natural language processing, contemporary computers can efficiently perform various tasks such as data summarization, sentence semantic similarity measurement, and text classification by utilizing sophisticated neural networks. Nevertheless, there is a growing need for computers to analyze data and perform operations on databases in various real-world domains such as finance, healthcare, and hospitality. To accomplish this, computers must execute complex SQL commands based on text inputs, a challenging task known as text-to-SQL. Notably, research on text-to-SQL has primarily focused on interior domains where training and application data originate from the same source and share the same data format. To address real-world scenarios, research must consider cross-domain settings where training and application data differ in both content and data structure. In response to this challenge, we propose a novel end-to-end, multi-task, text-to-SQL framework capable of incorporating auxiliary tasks to enhance primary database query generation performance. In particular, we employ classification and summary tasks as auxiliary tasks to augment the primary text-to-SQL task by leveraging both global and record-level semantic information. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation metric, known as execution accuracy, in addition to the conventional exact match ratio. In benchmark tests using ADSTable, a publicly available dataset suitable for assessing table schema understanding and database query generation from text inputs, our proposed method achieves execution accuracy and exact match ratios that surpass existing records. The central theme of this research can be expressed as trying to understand how the structure of these samples is affected by two opposing forces: their internal consistency and how they relate to the broader dataset they were drawn from. In statistics, this is known as the interplay between within-series and external variability. To investigate this dynamic in language models, we selected random words from corpora at irregular intervals and examined how they compare to the overall language pattern. Our findings reveal that even in highly structured contexts, such as natural language, the words we drew at random exhibited significant variation compared to the overall pattern, and this within-series diversity cannot be accurately predicted without taking their internal consistency into account. Interestingly, when we applied the same approach to synthetic data with intentionally introduced randomness, our results showed that the words we drew at random demonstrated remarkably high internal consistency and, in many cases, could be accurately predicted based on their own structure rather than the broader dataset they were drawn from. Our research used a simple neural network model to simulate the generation of words and found that increasing the random variation during generation resulted in words that were both more internally consistent and more distinct from the broader dataset. To further explore the relationship between the size and complexity of datasets and the structure of the samples drawn from them, we applied the principles of macrosequences and deviation principles to identify specific patterns and distributions that these samples adhere to. In doing so, we discovered that the distribution of the words we drew at random conformed to a specific statistical pattern known as super-Poisson dynamics when the dataset itself exhibited the same distribution, but switched to a different pattern known as sub-Poisson dynamics when the dataset did not share the same distribution. When we limited the random variation during generation to its most basic form, the words that resulted shared the same distribution as the broader dataset they were drawn from, but only up to a certain point, after which they switched to a different distribution known as the Gruby-Lanford distribution. Our research also found that the words we drew at random exhibited distinct patterns based on their position within the sequence, with the words at the beginning and end of the sequence sharing different distributions than the words in the middle. In response to the growing interest in these frameworks, there has been a corresponding increase in novel approaches being proposed and published. To provide a clear path through this growing body of work, this survey carefully examines and categorizes the numerous proposed methods, exploring their potential to tackle challenging issues in machine learning, natural language processing, and related fields. By reviewing and classifying the existing literature, this survey aims to offer valuable insights for both practicing engineers and research academics in search of innovative techniques to tackle various data analysis problems. In addition to reviewing and classifying the existing research, this survey also explores the potential risks and limitations of the proposed approaches, as well as potential avenues for future research and development.

This challenge is particularly pronounced in the development of quantum threshold logic, as it requires the reliable detection of the absorption of a single photon. This study examines the impact of recoil caused by photon absorption on the quantum states of individual strontium atoms within a cloud of trapped atoms and explores alternative beam absorption measurement techniques that can minimize or sidestep this issue. This research provides a theoretical framework for modeling beam absorption in the presence of recoil and demonstrates the feasibility of detecting lost photons through the measurement of momentum distribution within the cloud of trapped atoms. This finding offers a practical solution to the problem of detecting the absorption of a single photon in quantum computing systems based on trapped and cooled atoms. This study also highlights the significance of incorporating momentum distribution measurements as a standard technique in absorption spectroscopy. This research was conducted using an apparatus that includes a cloud of trapped strontium atoms, a beam of light, a camera to capture images of the cloud, and a device to measure momentum distribution, and it resulted in the creation of a detailed chart of beam absorption in the presence of recoil. This chart can be utilized by other researchers working with different types of atoms and molecules. This study demonstrated the feasibility of detecting the absorption of a single photon in quantum computing systems based on trapped and cooled atoms and provided a detailed framework for modeling beam absorption in the presence of recoil that can be applied to other systems. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of viscoelastic materials exhibit a sudden and extreme thickening in their fluids, resulting in a transition from rapid flow to near immobility. Until now, this dramatic phenomenon, known as shear thickening, has been poorly understood on a global scale due to the limitations of available measurement techniques. Using a novel approach that utilizes a large range of shear rates, our research reveals the universal characteristics of this transition and reveals a previously unknown, simple relationship between shear stress and shear rate that applies across all measurements. By interpreting these findings through the lens of jamming theory, we gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanics and identify the precise point at which the shear thickening transition begins, as well as the factors that influence it. Furthermore, our data reveals two distinct shear thickening behaviors that reflect diverse microscopical phenomena, including the interaction between polymer chains and particulate jamming. By applying our findings to real-world scenarios, our research highlights the potential for materials exhibiting this phenomenon to be optimized for a broader range of applications. Lastly, our results underscore the crucial role played by particle interactions at stresses that far exceed those required to initiate the shear thickening transition.

Web search engines such as Google prioritize results based on users' past searching behavior, which may cause certain websites with high authority to be favored over others with equal or even superior content. This personalization can lead to a significant issue: it overlooks pertinent information outside of users' usual searching channels. We conducted an experiment that searched for individuals who had searched for information related to a misleading news article but were not redirected to corrective information on popular websites. We found that a substantial number of these individuals were not exposed to fact-checking websites, even when they were directly accessible through simple additional search queries. Our data suggests that up to 29% of such individuals remained unaware of existing fact-checking content. These findings underscore the risks associated with Web search personalization and highlight the need for search engines to balance customization with discovery of novel information. Ultimately, our results support previous theoretical concerns about the limitations of Web search personalization and provide actionable insights for search engine optimization and algorithm design. Our research also offers a method for evaluating search engines' ability to uncover novel information and detects a phenomenon we call "information isolation." When faced with unfamiliar terms, search engines prioritize established knowledge over novel information, prioritizing websites that have been visited or referenced frequently in the past. Our findings suggest that up to 53% of individuals may overlook relevant information due to this phenomenon. Our results are relevant to a broad range of applications, including search engine optimization, algorithm design, online misinformation remediation, and educational initiatives. Our research highlights the need for further study into the interplay between search engine personalization, user behavior, and online information discovery. The paired-permutation test in statistical analysis has a limiting factor due to its sequential nature, which can hinder the simultaneous testing of many hypotheses. To overcome this constraint, this paper introduces an efficient method for testing multiple paired hypotheses using a paired-permutation test in a single permutation calculation. A novel paired-permutation test statistic called the "precise paired-permutation" (PPPM) is derived, which enables the simultaneous testing of multiple paired hypotheses using a single permutation calculation. By applying the PPPM method, we demonstrate significant reductions in computational time required for testing multiple paired hypotheses using a paired-permutation test. Furthermore, the PPPM method yields test statistics with a known distribution, which facilitates the use of critical values for scaling the test to a desired level of significance. To evaluate and compare the performance of the PPPM method with existing alternatives, we conducted numerical experiments using both synthetic and real-world data sets. The results obtained from these experiments confirm the efficiency and effectiveness of the PPPM method, which outperforms existing alternatives in terms of both computational time and accuracy. The code developed for this research has been publicly released on GitHub, which can be utilized for implementing the PPPM method for both paired and unpaired permutation tests. The code is also suitable for use with large data sets. The term "precise paired-permutation examination" (PPEX) refers to the general class of methods to which the PPPM method belongs, which includes the PPPM method as a specific instance. The PPEX framework provides a platform for developing and assessing new variants of the PPPM method. The code developed for this research is also compatible with the R environment. The PPEX method has been successfully applied to real-world data sets in various fields, which are presented in the supplementary material. The PPEX method can be extended to multiway permutation tests, which are a more general class of tests than paired permutation tests. The derivation of the exact distribution of the test statistic for multiway permutation tests using the PPEX method remains an open research question. The development of an efficient algorithm for scaling the PPEX method to accommodate large data sets also presents an area for further research. We investigate the potential of future $e^+e^-$ colliders operating at TeV energies to detect double Higgs boson production resulting from new physics beyond the Standard Model, using Effective Field Theory as a framework for new physics. Due to the significant interference between the standard electroweak double Higgs production process and contributions from new physics, we examine the impact of BSM Higgs interactions that violate the custodial symmetry, specifically those leading to $HZZ$ and $HHZZ$ couplings, in order to determine their observable effects on double Higgs production in $e^+e^-$ collisions. We calculate the production cross-sections for double Higgs bosons in these colliders, taking into consideration the detector acceptance and identifying the most promising signatures for detecting these processes. We also determine the required center-of-mass energy for 1-fb $e^+e^-$ collision data to achieve a discovery or precision measurement of the $HZZ$ and $HHZZ$ couplings, including an assessment of the impact of polarization for initial state electrons and positrons. We investigate the drag experienced by an elongated cylindrical object moving through a bed of granular material, specifically with varying levels of fluid saturation, from completely dry to partially and fully saturated conditions. Previous research has examined the dynamics of individual grains and a single, large solid cylinder within a dry granular medium but not extensively the anisotropic effects of drag on a long, thin cylinder across different saturation levels. Our experiments with a range of saturated conditions, varying cylinder lengths and widths, and different granular material properties reveal significant anisotropic drag forces, influenced by the relationship between the cylinder's dimensions and the granular material's properties. We found that the drag force can be anisotropic even in saturated conditions, contrary to previous knowledge. Our data are correlated using an anisotropic friction law that takes into account the normal force, the angle of friction, and the ratio of the cylinder's height to its width. We also discuss the implications of these findings on the object's dynamics and interactions with the surrounding granular material bed. Moreover, our results highlight the significance of proper dimensionless analysis in order to accurately interpret and generalize the findings from our experiments. Lastly, we examine the effects of increased saturation on the drag forces and the object's dynamics, revealing that the object's behavior can be described by a dimensionless number that combines the effects of fluid saturation and the angle of friction. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between solid grains, fluid, and a moving object within a saturated granular medium.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, applying it to 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, identical in nature to $v_2/\epsilon_2$. These findings conformed to Buda-London theory, which link anisotropic initial conditions, interactions, and resulting anisotropic flows through systems' universal properties. Verification of our results was achieved by comparing our data to the coefficients derived from individual particle measurements within the same transport model. Additionally, we calculated triangular flow for 1.73 GeV Au+Au collisions and found it to be roughly 50% lower than its 200 GeV counterpart. Lastly, our analysis revealed that initial anisotropic geometry exhibited a triangular structure in Au+Au collisions, consistent with random geometric patterns.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a particular interest in developing methods that preserve positivity, conserve flux, or maintain a specific dissipative behavior. Although implicit conservation laws, positivity-preserving, and monotonicity-preserving methods have been extensively studied, their implementation through iterative techniques such as the generalized minimum residual (GMRES) method poses significant challenges due to the absence of explicit expressions for solution updates. This paper addresses this issue by developing a preconditioned GMRES method for approximating solutions to a broad class of time-dependent scalar conservation laws, where the method ensures preservation of a dissipative behavior for a specific norm. A key aspect of this approach involves utilizing the existing knowledge of GMRES methods to efficiently determine suitable parameters that ensure preservation of the desired property of the approximate solutions. Understanding the intricacies of organ development and pathologies often requires the visualization and analysis of complex three-dimensional surfaces. Acquiring such surfaces through non-invasive imaging techniques like computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging is straightforward but can lead to registration inaccuracies due to limited data and the soft, curved nature of organs. A non-rigid registration method based on a linear elasticity model has shown promise in aligning volumetric data with surface data but may not accurately capture the detailed morphology evident in corrected volumes. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed that leverages a linear elasticity model in conjunction with a volume-to-surface registration method to align soft organ volumes and surfaces, relying on the assumption that the organs' mechanical properties remain relatively constant across different subjects and developmental stages. By utilizing a sparse and distributed finite element approach, the method achieves faster computation times and enables the registration of large datasets. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method on real MRI datasets, yielding registration accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art non-rigid methods while significantly reducing computation time. Furthermore, the proposed method facilitates the computation of surface mechanical parameters from volumetric data, eliminating the need for a separate estimation step and providing an alternative to existing machine learning-based prediction methods. By integrating the proposed method with a level set surface evolution framework, the research also presents an application for solving a challenging volume-to-surface registration problem involving the alignment of complex organ volumes and surfaces, with the aim of removing surface irregularities from real-world medical images. The proposed method and application have been made available online as open-source software. The research demonstrates the potential of linear elasticity-based models in conjunction with volume-to-surface registration methods to accurately capture the detailed morphology of soft organs, with implications for various biomedical applications. The findings also highlight the feasibility of using a biomechanical model to infer surface irregularities from volumetric data, with the potential for extension to related problems in fields like computer vision and robotics. The proposed method has been evaluated and compared with a range of state-of-the-art registration methods, with the option for users to modify the comparison based on different performance metrics. The research has been conducted within the framework of a publicly accessible dataset involving pediatric brain images, with the potential for application to adult brain images and other biomedical domains. The proposed method has been designed to accommodate various mesh-based surface representations, with extensions possible to other surface formats and related problems in fields like computer vision and robotics. The research has been conducted with the support of a computational grant, with implications for various large-scale biomedical applications.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for each point in an image by considering both stereo and optical flow information. Although several deep learning approaches have improved stereo and optical flow estimation techniques, their individual limitations significantly impact the accuracy of scene flow estimation. To address this challenge, we propose a self-guided approach that leverages a unique adversarial network to compare the plausibility of estimated motion vectors in relation to other points within an image. By doing so, it learns a metric that accurately represents the spatial coherence of motion, leading to improved flow boundaries and reduced noise in the estimated motion trajectories. Compared to conventional metric learning methods, our adversarial network effectively handles the imbalance between background points and points with valid motion trajectories, resulting in a 5% absolute improvement in the evaluation score. Additionally, our method enhances the spatial coherence of both optical and stereo flow estimates, resulting in a 6% and 10% absolute improvement in the evaluation scores, respectively. By utilizing only a single stereo image, our approach achieves a 10% absolute improvement in the evaluation score compared to current state-of-the-art methods that utilize two stereo images.
