Contemporary microservices utilize containerized services for developing and deploying applications at high speed. As the number of services grows, managing permissions across individual containers becomes an escalating challenge. Existing solutions either overgrant broad permissions or are too restrictive, compromising security or efficiency respectively. In response, we present Timeloops, an innovative, self-governing policy learning approach for containerized microservices. The Timeloops framework automatically generates and refines access control policies in response to changes in system calls made by individual containers during operation. By analyzing past system calls and predicting future behavior, the Timeloops framework creates a predictive model that streamlines policy enforcement and minimizes unnecessary permission adjustments. In evaluation tests involving real-world applications, Timeloops reduces average permission overhead by approximately 70% and successfully implements policies with nearly identical efficacy to manual configurations. Timeloops' lightweight, automated design, coupled with its capacity to balance security and efficiency, positions it as a cutting-edge solution for the increasingly prevalent containerized microservices landscape. Timeloops' lightweight, self-governing approach can balance security and efficiency in containerized microservices environments. Timeloops' code is available online at https://github.com/ucy-cyber/timeloops-containers. Reverse time migration has been highly successful for years, however its most advanced version, amplified source waveform inversion, has not been widely applied due to its high computational cost and instability issues, especially when using large time-step sizes. In amplified source waveform inversion, additional terms are added to the classical wave equation to account for source and receiver recordings, which results in the system matrix becoming fully populated and computationally expensive to solve. To address this limitation, we propose a new method that reformulates the amplified source wave equation using the Kirchhoff approximation, which significantly reduces the system matrix sparsity and yields promising results in simulated data. In particular, using the proposed method with a large time-step size (0.75 ms) leads to a 2 times speedup in computation compared to the classical wave equation solver when using a small time-step size (0.5 ms). Notably, the proposed method also produces comparable image quality to the classical amplified source waveform inversion. We further investigate the impact of the Kirchhoff approximation parameter by conducting numerical experiments and find that a moderate value (10) strikes a balance between reduced computation and image quality. To assess the applicability of the proposed method to real data, we apply it to the Marmousi2 model and obtain a satisfactory result. We provide a detailed proof of a recent statement regarding the solvability of certain systems of congruences modulo prime powers, specifically those involving Hecke algebra equations and ideal class group relations for an algebraic number theory extension of Q. This proof builds upon the fundamental work of Leopoldt, by establishing the solvability of such systems and establishing connections to the rationality of Dirichlet L-series. Additionally, we offer explicit bounds for the indices of solvability and rationality, thereby expanding on earlier related results due to Michel and Ellenberg. Furthermore, we offer a corrected and simplified proof of a related statement found in an earlier study by the first author. Lastly, we discuss the implications and potential applications of these results to other related problems. This research was inspired by the ideas presented in a lecture by Michel during the 2010 AIM Summer Graduate School on Algebraic Number Theory.

In this work, we examine the capabilities of Belle II to detect and exclude light dark photons mediated by an Axion-Like Particle (ALP) through the study of specific $B$ meson decays into leptons and mesons. By utilizing a comprehensive set of production and decay processes at Belle II, we determine the ALP mass range that the experiment can reach with a 5.5 ab$^{-1}$ data sample. Our findings indicate that Belle II can achieve sensitivities as low as $0.13\cdot10^{-3}$ eV for a 0.01 decay-in-flight lifetime and $0.53\cdot10^{-3}$ eV for a 0.1 production-in-meson lifetime in its ideal configuration. We also explore the impact of hadronic uncertainties and pileup, as well as various $B$ meson production modes, in order to ensure a comprehensive evaluation of the ALP discovery reach in $e^+e^-\to B\bar{B}$ at Belle II. As expected, we find that the detection of ALPs at Belle II will be more effective for $B$ decays that produce final states with significant energy, such as those involving tau or charm leptons. Furthermore, we discuss the connection between Belle II's capabilities and LHC searches for similar ALP signatures in proton-proton collisions. As a result of these studies, we propose new observable channels for Belle II and suggest additional analyses of $B$ decays into vector bosons and heavy mesons for the purpose of enhancing the ALP discovery reach in $e^+e^-\to B\bar{B}$ at the Belle II experiment. With these proposals, we anticipate that Belle II will be capable of detecting ALPs with masses as low as $26.4$ meV, subject to a specific decay-in-meson lifetime and heavy meson production modes. Consequently, we believe that the study of $B$ decays into heavy mesons at the Belle II experiment has the potential to significantly expand the reach of low-energy beam dump experiments, such as the SHiP and LHCb beam dump modes, in the search for light long-lived states. This modified version, which we call the quantum relational Hoare calculus, utilizes a concept called "expectation" to ensure that the truth of a post condition in a program's context is linked to the truth of the corresponding condition in the program itself. We have further expanded the calculus to accommodate programs that incorporate operations to move quantum information around. Additionally, we have demonstrated how this calculus can be used in conjunction with Verifiable C Compiler to ensure the quantum safety of compiled programs. Moreover, we have explored the application of the quantum relational Hoare calculus to solve reachability problems in multi-qubit programs. This involves creating a method to track the evolution of a specific program property, represented as a relation, through the program's execution. This can be achieved by mapping the program's transition function into a form that is amenable to analysis using the relational Hoare calculus, effectively allowing us to determine the earliest point in time at which a particular state becomes acceptable as it evolves over time. This discovery provides a solution to the broader problem of identifying the shortest path from an initial state to a target state. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases often rely on a small number of individuals with whom others have extensive contact, a phenomenon we are referring to as super-spreader events in this context. While these events are well-documented in various settings such as transportation, gatherings and crowded environments, the limited number of people involved in them typically makes them difficult to incorporate into mathematical modeling. This paper discusses a new modeling approach that takes into consideration the super-spreader events by assigning a large number of contacts to a minority of infectors at random. By simulating and analyzing a susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed model with this feature, we observe that it leads to a much faster epidemic peak compared to traditional models, as well as a significantly larger total number of infected individuals, even when the average number of contacts is relatively low. This is further confirmed by comparing it to a model that includes a non-linear transmission probability, also resulting in a shorter peak time and more infected individuals. This modeling approach and its analysis provide valuable insights into various epidemic control measures, showing that reducing the size of super-spreader events, improving personal protection measures or increasing isolation measures can all significantly slow down and limit the spread of the disease. This modeling approach can also be applied to modeling the spread of diseases in more complex networks. This paper also discusses some possible extensions to modeling the spread of diseases in geographical areas. This model and its analysis provide valuable data that can be used in conjunction with real-world data to better understand and manage the spread of diseases. This is demonstrated by simulating and analyzing the spread of SARS in Hong Kong, resulting in estimates of crucial parameters that can be used to manage and control similar epidemics in the future. This paper also discusses some possible extensions to modeling the spread of diseases in random networks. This includes modeling the spread of diseases in networks with different types of nodes, as well as adapting this model to simulate the spread of diseases in online social networks. This paper also discusses some possible policy implications of this model, including the optimal timing for implementing control measures during an epidemic, which can be determined by calculating the critical point at which implementing control measures will result in significant health and economic benefits. This paper also discusses some possible extensions to modeling the spread of diseases in changing environments, which can be achieved by adapting this model to include time-dependent parameters. This paper also discusses some possible extensions to modeling the spread of diseases in networks with different types of nodes, which can be achieved by adapting this model to include node-specific transmission probabilities. Automated techniques for estimating the vector magnetic field in solar imaging have achieved remarkable precision, however, a potential issue with these methods, especially using local photospheric techniques, has been identified. It was found that, when applying a specific technique to a particular plasma feature type, it consistently produces inaccurate measurements for certain magnetic field characteristics. This study investigates the inherent biases in a particular estimation method, specifically the local photospheric technique, and explores ways to correct it. By developing a statistical model, the study uncovers the presence of persistent biases in the estimated measurements and identifies their sources as variations in plasma conditions and the geometry of magnetic field lines. To alleviate these biases, the researchers developed a de-biasing technique and tested it on synthetic data, finding it to be effective in both linear and nonlinear scenarios. When applied to real solar data using the local photospheric technique, the study reveals that the primary plasma condition influencing the estimation error is the gradient of the magnetic field, and it recommends a specific correction method to reduce the estimation error. By implementing this correction, the study demonstrates a significant reduction in estimation error, from approximately 40% to less than 10%. Consequently, this study highlights the importance of accounting for plasma conditions when estimating the vector magnetic field and provides a practical solution for correcting the local photospheric technique used in solar imaging. Transfer learning in deep neural networks enables effective utilization across related tasks by leveraging previously acquired knowledge. However, our research reveals that this technique is not consistently effective for dissimilar tasks, such as adapting a classification model for image classification to generate natural language descriptions. To address this limitation, we propose a novel, unsupervised method known as RETRACE, which leverages unlabelled data from the target domain to improve the representation learning for a pre-trained model employed in a range of tasks. Specifically, RETRACE employs a contrastive technique to fine-tune the model by incorporating features extracted from encoders utilized in other tasks and domain-specific data. Consequently, RETRACE enables our proposed approach to excel in various cross-task scenarios, such as describing natural scenes after being trained on product descriptions. We validate RETRACE through a series of rigorous experiments across multiple tasks and domains, and the findings consistently support our claims that RETRACE consistently boosts performance compared to the baseline transfer learning technique. Moreover, RETRACE excels even when compared to supervised methods employed as baselines, thereby underscoring its value as a highly cost-effective solution. Finally, we make the code and models publicly available for further research and development.

Lately, various neural networks have been applied to sensitive data by the industry and academia, thus leading to a growing interest in the field of differential privacy. Although there have been significant advancements in developing private neural networks, one critical challenge remains - choosing the optimal hyperparameters for training. This issue is compounded by the significant computational costs associated with training and evaluating neural networks, as well as the added expense of conducting multiple privacy attacks to validate the efficacy of private neural networks in a production setting. To address these concerns, this paper presents a novel method for efficiently tuning hyperparameters for neural networks in a private setting using a reduced number of training data. We leverage a combination of Bayesian optimization and a robust privacy attack to efficiently tune hyperparameters for a private neural network with guaranteed differential privacy. Experimental results on popular neural network architectures demonstrate significant improvements in tuning efficiency without compromising performance, as well as the added benefit of transferring learned hyperparameters to new, unseen data with minimal additional tuning required. Our code is publicly available online. Moreover, we provide a private neural network training platform that includes pre-trained models and hyperparameter tuning for new datasets, thus facilitating seamless industry adoption. This approach has been successfully applied to real-world data in the industry, thus we also present an industrial-scale case study on the hyperparameter tuning of a large-scale neural network used by Uber Eats. Our findings have significant implications for the effective deployment of private neural networks in a production setting with limited data and computational resources available. We also discuss the added expense of conducting multiple privacy attacks and possible alternatives to Bayesian optimization that could further enhance the efficiency of hyperparameter tuning for neural networks in a private setting. We conclude by examining the limitations of this approach and potential avenues for further research, thus providing a foundation for the development of efficient hyperparameter tuning for neural networks in a private setting. In this work, a group G is defined as having a boolean structure if its involutions form a boolean subgroup. We then explore various properties of such groups and establish connections to other boolean-related characteristics. Specifically, we demonstrate that G's boolean structure is equivalent to the conjugacy of its subgroups consisting of pairs of transpositions that commute with each other. This condition in turn is identical to the conjugacy of all 2-subsets of G's elements, which results in G being isomorphic to the symmetric group S8. This specific structure of S8(s) is also shown to be unique by proving that any finite group that has both a boolean structure and 2-transitivity is precisely S8(n). Finally, we examine the implications of a finite group's boolean structure for its irreducible characters and obtain a characterization of its character degrees. This characterization leads to a lower bound on the number of a finite group's irreducible characters when that group has a boolean structure. This in turn enables us to determine the finite groups with the fewest irreducible characters when they have a boolean structure and show that these groups are consistently symmetic groups of the form S8(n). The rapid spread of medical misinformation and conspiracy theories in China, fueled by social media, posed a significant challenge in combating the COVID-19 pandemic. To address this issue, the Chinese government launched a special rumor-refuting campaign, employing influential online figures known as "opinion leaders" to counter false information and promote verifiable health guidelines. By examining data collected through online surveillance and crowdsourcing, our research explored the mechanisms underlying the dissemination of health rumors and assessed the campaign's effectiveness. We gathered data on 383 verified health rumors and identified key factors contributing to their spread, including characteristics of the rumors themselves, the opinions and behaviors of online users, and the official responses to the pandemic. We also evaluated the campaign's impact by analyzing the influence of opinion leaders who refuted the rumors and explored how the government's pandemic policies affected the spread of future rumors. Our study revealed that the most prevalent health rumors in China, as in other countries, are associated with conspiracy theories and misinformation about the COVID-19 virus, symptoms, and treatments. We found that older users, those with lower levels of education, and individuals who distrust the government are more susceptible to spreading health rumors. We also discovered that the campaign led by opinion leaders was more successful in preventing the further dissemination of already identified health rumors but was less effective in detecting and addressing new ones. Our research highlights the critical role that opinion leaders play in containing the spread of health misinformation during the pandemic and suggests that the government's measures to combat the pandemic, such as lockdowns and travel restrictions, can actually contribute to the increased dissemination of false information among remaining online populations. We propose a framework for assessing the impact of medical misinformation on individuals and the broader society and discuss the implications of our findings for public health policies aimed at curbing the spread of medical misinformation in China during the COVID-19 pandemic. We also examine the broader societal consequences of conspiracy theories and misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic and discuss the applicability of our research to other medical crises and epidemics in China and beyond. We believe that our research provides a foundation for further studies on the dynamics of medical misinformation in China during the COVID-19 pandemic and offers actionable policy recommendations for public health officials, healthcare professionals, and technology industry leaders working together to combat the spread of medical misinformation in China and globally. We hope that our research will contribute to the development of effective strategies for preventing the spread of medical misinformation and promoting public health and safety in China and other countries facing similar challenges. We also hope that our research will shed light on the broader societal consequences

A search for planetary nebulae (PNe) in the Fornax cluster was conducted by cross-matching the S$^4$G and VEGAS surveys, resulting in the identification of 540 PNe associated with early-type galaxies within the cluster. Using a customized PNe scaling relation, the absolute magnitudes of 380 PNe in elliptical galaxies were determined, and a mean distance of 15.9 megaparsecs to the cluster was calculated with a margin of error of 0.7 megaparsecs. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of data from medical devices, electrophysiology, and imaging equipment. These datasets, described as high-dimensional time series, hold significant clinical potential if analyzed effectively. However, processing such data on platforms like Apache Spark Streaming and Flink proves to be resource-intensive and impractical for real-time applications on limited infrastructure. Existing solutions either sacrifice low latency for cost efficiency or vice versa without a middle ground. In response, we present a custom-designed engine, called LifeStream, tailored to efficiently handle periodic data processing tasks on a high dimensionality time series. By leveraging periodic task consolidation, in-place updates, and a customized memory management system, LifeStream achieves significant reductions in memory usage and processing time. In our experiments using real-world medical data from the PhysioNet Challenge 2012, LifeStream demonstrates improved performance compared to Spark Streaming and Flink, using both simulated and actual hospital data. As a result, LifeStream can be an efficient and reliable platform for real-time data analysis across various medical applications. In addition to medical data, LifeStream's architecture also enables efficient processing of other periodic time series workloads. Additionally, this category's parameters are linked to the original Bertrand curve's characteristics. Lastly, this paper demonstrates that the (1,3)-Bertrand curve evolves from a specific differential equation when the standard Sarlet-Bertrand equation is altered. Similar connections to other curve types, such as hyper surface curves and curves in a hypersurface, are also established. This study's findings are further applied to a specific curve, resulting in a new solution to the differential equation originally solved by Cartan and later generalized by Blair. The simulation successfully replicated the injection molding process and produced results that agreed with experimental data, including density, crystallinity, and melting heat measurements. Furthermore, the simulation revealed distinct zones within the molded part, characterized by varying levels of crystallinity, shear strain, temperature, and molecular orientation. These findings support the utility of this simulation model in predicting and controlling the microstructure development and resulting properties of injection-molded polymers undergoing SIC. Previous research relied heavily on training and retrieving from vast information spaces, without fully accounting for the fundamental principles of which knowledge serves as a foundation. To address this, we assembled the ATOMIC database, a comprehensive collection of causal relationships that can be used to assess various intelligent behaviors, such as determining causality and evaluating consequences. This database allows us to explore the connection between the scale and diversity of knowledge and the complexity of underlying models, revealing that a subset of ATOMIC containing 200 simple causal relationships suffices to capture a wide range of complex behaviors exhibited by state-of-the-art models. When evaluated against this atlas, current models fail to generalize beyond the boundaries of their training data, demonstrating that current models do not possess a general understanding of the world but rather rely on memorized specifics of individual instances. When equipped with this atlas, however, they are able to exhibit intelligent behaviors that extend far beyond their initial training. Despite its limitations, the ATOMIC database also reveals that current models are capable of accurately reproducing intricate patterns of intelligent behavior rooted in machine common knowledge. Although HHL impressively minimizes pre-processing time to a logarithmic scale, its slow scaling of post-processing time, influenced by the magnitude of matrix dimensions, could hinder its practical applications. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel hybrid Quantum-Classical Linear Algebra (NISQ-HHL) protocol that dynamically adjusts the quantum post-processing duration in direct proportion to the square root of matrix dimensions. By optimally managing the size of a limited quantum resource basket, we successfully enhance the performance of HHL in the medium-term quantum era. Specifically, our findings indicate that in the regime where the number of qubits is constrained to 3-5, the NISQ-HHL variant outperforms its standard counterpart by several orders of magnitude, solving large-scale linear algebra problems that are otherwise inaccessible with current quantum technology. Predicting video content from non-rigid and dynamic viewpoints is a complex task 
that has a wide range of practical applications including surveillance, video editing 
and augmented reality. In this research, we introduce a novel task called view video 
forecasting that involves dynamically changing the viewpoint of a video over time. We 
also present a new view video forecasting method that employs a dual representation 
approach to anticipate both the viewpoint and the corresponding video frame. In our method, 
a dual representation model is trained to produce both the target frame and the target 
viewpoint, and it is further developed into a dynamic version that can be used for view 
video forecasting. We validate our approach on a newly created dataset for view video 
forecasting and achieve superior results compared to baseline methods. Additionally, we 
utilize the view video forecasting capability to enhance the effectiveness of a specific 
object detection method and achieve improved performance on multiple benchmarks. The 
code for our research is publicly accessible on GitHub.

Airborne transmission of illnesses within enclosed environments is a complex and poorly understood process that varies depending on several factors, including respiration rate, viral droplet size, and how aerosols mix in the air. We examine the validity of a widely used, simplified model that assumes uniform mixing of airborne pathogens and test its limitations using a more realistic computational model that accounts for turbulence and particle dynamics. By comparing the two models in a controlled setting, such as a city bus, we investigate how the models' differences affect their ability to predict aerosol particle distribution and how they relate to illness transmission risk. Our findings suggest that a model assuming perfect mixing may overestimate transmission risks by as much as five times and highlight the importance of considering the actual dynamics of aerosol transport and the physical characteristics of infected individuals when assessing the spread of airborne pathogens. By taking these factors into consideration, we can develop more effective strategies for mitigating the transmission of illnesses in enclosed environments. Our research also provides a detailed, open-source simulation tool that allows for precise simulation of aerosol particle distribution in complex environments. Our results have implications for various settings beyond urban buses, including offices, restaurants, and public transportation systems. By better understanding the behavior of aerosol transmission dynamics, we can develop more accurate and effective models for predicting and controlling the spread of airborne pathogens in urban environments. The beam disruption effect causes oscillations in the electric potential of an energy recovery linac's bunching system when a spent beam interacts with a remaining beam. This phenomenon can result in unstable oscillations in the system's electric potential and potentially lead to bunching system instability. The filling configuration of an energy recovery linac, specifically how the remaining and spent beams are arranged in the ring, influences the beam disruption instability's severity. This study investigates how different filling configurations impact the beam disruption instability and explores strategies to minimize the effect and ensure the safe operation of an energy recovery linac. This research leverages a previously developed theoretical model that accounts for the complex interactions between the ring's electric potential, the beam's electric field, and the ring's geometry, and it applies this model to a specific energy recovery linac known as the Advanced Proton Source. This facility is part of Brookhaven National Laboratory's upgrade to the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. The analysis of the Advanced Proton Source reveals that energy recovery linacs are highly susceptible to beam disruption instability but also shows that carefully selecting the filling configuration can minimize this effect and keep its impact below a critical threshold. For the Advanced Proton Source, choosing a filling configuration where the same beam type occupies adjacent bunches reduces the impact of beam disruption instability by more than ten times over a configuration where the remaining and spent beams are arranged alternately. This study's findings underscore the significance of thoroughly examining an energy recovery linac's filling configuration as part of its operational safety assessment. The behavior of molten polymer bristles under strong stretching forces has been extensively studied, and research has focused on the mechanics of individual bristles as well as collections of bristles within complex materials. Previous studies have examined the mechanics of isolated bristles with varying levels of surface roughness, finding that stretched bristles create exclusion zones around them, similar to how solid objects create voids in molten materials. The current study expands upon this knowledge by investigating the mechanics of multiple bristles with complex shapes, varying surface roughness, and different orientations, even in situations where bristles intersect one another. By simulating and analyzing these scenarios using finite element modeling, we discovered that the exclusion zones around bristles can vary in size, but generally, they maintain a constant proportion to the scale of the bristle itself. Additionally, we found that the exclusion zones do not significantly change when bristles are bent or when surface roughness is introduced. However, combining highly curved bristles together results in exclusion zones that overlap and eventually merge into a single, continuous void when the bristles are very curved. This research provides computational evidence for the idea that the exclusion zones around bristles are determined by their local curvature rather than specific shapes, and it offers insights into the materials science of polymer bristles and their collections. This includes suggestions for creating materials with controlled void spaces and further proposed experiments using bristles with designed shapes and surface features. The metric dimension of a graph measures the minimum number of markers required to uniquely identify vertices based on distance information. We introduce a new parameter, half-dimensional sets, which determines the minimum number of markers needed for a 2-dimensional distinguishing power equivalent to the original metric dimension. We establish guidelines for determining the half-dimensional and metric dimensions for graphs and show their equivalence in specific instances, such as particular tree structures and certain grid configurations. Furthermore, we examine half-dimensional and metric dimensions in connection with other graph parameters and discover their relationship to minimum dominating sets, vertex cover, and clique number. Additionally, we establish upper and lower bounds for half-dimensional and metric dimensions and explore their connection to the number of distinct distances and maximum degree. Lastly, we determine the half-dimensional and metric dimensions of hypercubes and provide a formula for their change when the graph changes from a line to a hypercube. We also include an open problem about the relationship between half-dimensional and metric dimensions.

Deep all-sky surveys like Fermi-GST produce vast amounts of data with varying sensitivity over the sky. To effectively analyze these to facilitate machine learning training, only regions with consistent signal detection are typically considered, leading to a less sensitive but more uniform data set. We trained a machine learning model on this sharper data set and found that, compared to the standard method using signal detection thresholds, it yielded a 2 times better performance in identifying variable sources and distinguishing them from non-variable ones. Moreover, the model's ability to identify source variability spectra was confirmed, indicating that the model is sensitive to source spectra and sky position information, not just data quality. This is particularly evident for sources with limited photon counts, demonstrating that machine learning can extract more information from the data than traditional methods based on count thresholds alone. This research demonstrates the potential benefits of training machine learning models on sharper data sets, enabling the analysis of less sensitive data regions and opening up new possibilities for discovering variable sources in deep surveys. This is especially relevant for future missions like AMBER and GAMMA-400 that will employ wide-field telescopes with lower photon collection limits. This project is an initial step towards developing a tool to automate detection of variable sources and can be improved by incorporating additional information, such as multi-wavelength data, high-energy theoretical models, and effective angular resolution. In a sequence of independent first-price auctions where the same bidder repeatedly competes as the last one standing, we examine how changes in auction format influence the bidder's expected payoff. Specifically, we compare the expected payoff from participating in a single first-price auction to the expected payoff from participating in the sequential auction structure. To generalize this scenario, we consider a broader "over" mechanism, in which bidders sequentially decide the order in which their individual valuation-maximizing actions will be taken, with the last action determining the final outcome. By exploring both positive and normative perspectives, our analysis offers insights into how various auction formats can be combined to create a more efficient sequence of actions. Our findings also provide upper and lower bounds on the optimal combined-auction payoff relative to the single-auction payoff. Furthermore, we investigate how the relationship between the two changes affects the difference between the expected payoffs from the over mechanism and the single auction. Our research builds upon prior works by Aumann and Kurz (1995), Jeroff (2013), and Macrelli and Teytelboym (2019).

We introduce a new, theoretically grounded approach to creating a generative conversational leader in Dungeons and Dragons. By drawing parallels between conversational management and game mechanics, we develop a framework where the leader's goals are represented as Intentions, and the players' motivations are estimated using Theory-of-Mind. To effectively guide the players, the dungeon master's actions are chosen to optimize alignment with the players' intended actions, influenced by their past behavior. We train a conversational agent using a combination of reinforcement learning and Intention-based control, which results in a significant improvement in assessing the players' Intentions and predicting their future actions. Human evaluations of our generated D&D scenarios reveal higher levels of engagement, cooperation, and enjoyment compared to a baseline random action selection model. When applied to real D&D sessions, our approach leads to a notable increase in alignment between the players' and the dungeon master's intended actions, as reported by the players themselves. A detailed investigation of a specific type of symmetry breaking, known as time-reversal or CP symmetry breaking, is conducted to understand the associated Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem within the context of both relativistic and non-relativistic quantum field theories. A particular time-reversal symmetry breaking scenario, characterized by the presence of a single massless fermionic NG boson and a set of massive scalar NG bosons, in both its real and complex forms, is explored through a comprehensive analysis of its impact on the theory's perturbative stability. The effects of symmetry breaking on the NG spectrum are then examined by perturbing the theory using a small symmetry-breaking parameter. The application of the $C$-operator technique allows for the identification of the NG fields and the derivation of a modified pole equation that includes the influence of the perturbing coupling. The resulting expression for the NG pole function is systematically constructed by employing both the $\epsilon$-regularization and $\Pi$-regularization methods. The analysis reveals that the presence of the perturbing coupling generates a term that violates the causality principle and leads to the creation of a scalar NG boson from the vacuum radiation, when the time-reversal symmetry breaking is achieved through the interaction with a fermionic NG boson. The connection between this phenomenon and the Jona-Lasinio model is also established. However, counterfactual data often takes a specific form that includes swapped action descriptions, making it challenging to produce on a large scale automatically. We address this challenge by developing a dataset that comprises over 13,000 pairs of news articles, in which a particular company is mentioned with either a positive or a negative aspect. We then design a method to generate counterfactual data automatically by swapping the polarity of action descriptions within short phrases, rather than at the sentence level. To evaluate this approach, we compare different language model fine-tuning methods and assess the quality of counterfactual data generated using these approaches. We find that fine-tuning models on tasks that involve identifying the polarity of action descriptions within short phrases results in a high level of accuracy, above 90%. This research focuses on a stochastic control problem where the cost function evolves in a discontinuous and unpredictable manner. Unlike conventional optimal control problems involving random disturbances, the uncertainty in this scenario affects the controller's ability to manipulate the system dynamically. Specifically, at any given time, the controller can choose one of two possible control actions, each with a distinct impact on the system's dynamics. The goal of the controller is to minimize expected costs over a finite-time horizon while taking into account the random nature of the cost function and the impact of the control actions on the system's dynamics. By utilizing a dual characterization and stochastic differential system methods, we establish the existence of an optimal control strategy that minimizes the expected cost of the system over the specified time horizon. Furthermore, we provide a detailed description of the optimal control solution, including explicit formulae for key variables, in both general and special cases. In addition to its inherent value, this research provides a solution to a previously unresolved problem posed by the reviewer in a prior study.

Mathematical modeling plays a significant role in managing and mitigating the spread of infectious diseases by providing critical information to public health officials. Different modeling approaches suit various purposes, including assessing epidemic potential, evaluating the effectiveness of control measures, and analyzing disease dynamics on a large scale. Epideomiological data is essential for developing and validating models, yet it can be challenging to obtain, especially in the early stages of an outbreak. This article discusses various modeling frameworks used to study the current COVID-19 pandemic, including ordinary differential equations, compartment models, stochastic simulations, and agent-based models, as well as their respective limitations and potential applications in guiding public health interventions. We have theoretically analyzed various methods for converting spinless atoms into molecules via three-body recombination. It is crucial to develop such a method as it could be a crucial step in achieving universal quantum gates with which trapped neutral atoms are equipped. Leveraging an example with which we are familiar, consisting of $^{87}$Rb atoms, we have determined the necessary conditions to achieve a high efficiency of spinor atom-molecule conversion. By utilizing a combination of coaxial beams to provide sufficient overlap between the recombination region and the detection zone, we have found that it is possible to achieve a high rate of atom-molecule conversion while minimizing the formation of two atoms per three-body recombination event. Furthermore, we have calculated the optimal beam intensity and position to maximize the molecule-atom recombination rate to approximately 10 times the three-body recombination rate observed in similar conditions. By implementing an atom-molecule conversion process based on two-beam configurations, with one beam inducing three-body recombination and the another beam detecting the molecule, we have determined that it is possible to achieve a rate of atom-molecule conversion as high as $10^4$ times the three-body recombination rate. By successfully developing this atom-molecule conversion technique, it could be applied to various other spinor atom-molecule conversion systems with which it is similar.

Understanding cardiac mechanics involves analyzing the electrical, contractual, and relaxation properties of heart muscle tissue.  Effective simulations rely on mathematical models that account for the electrical and contractual activities of the heart, but these simulations can be computationally expensive and difficult to scale due to the complex interactions and varying timeframes of the underlying systems. As a result, developing efficient and accurate solvers for the partial differential equations governing cardiac mechanics is crucial. One key factor in efficient solvers is the linear system solver used to solve the fast electrical propagation equations, with the speed and scalability of these solvers determining the overall simulation time. This study compares the performance of three such solvers the Generalized Minimum Residual (GMRES) with a preconditioner based on the Direct Amplification of Advancement Block-Toeplitz matrix, the Conjugate Gradient Method with a multilevel Fast Fourier Transform-based preconditioner, and the BiConjugate Gradient squared Method with a multilevel Fourier preconditioner to solve the monodomain and reduced activety models of cardiac electromechanics mechanics using the OpenCVM package. Our results show that the GMRES solver with the Direct Amplification of Advancement Block-Toeplitz matrix preconditioner outperforms the other two solvers in terms of simulation time and memory usage, with further analysis indicating that the slow simulation time is primarily due to the reduced activety model rather than the electrophysiology solver used. Our findings also confirm that the monodomain model is more computationally expensive than the reduced activety model but scales more efficiently with the number of heart muscle cells simulated. Our results have important implications for the development of efficient and accurate solvers for cardiac mechanics simulations. Multiple evaluation environments are proposed to facilitate meaningful assessments of lifelong learning methods.

Determining the precise mechanisms driving galaxy evolution, particularly the decline of star formation in massive galaxies, remains a complex issue that has been debated among scientists for a long time. By examining a large sample of 1.4 GHz Giant Metre Wave Radio Telescope Synthesis Telescope (GMRT-SRT) observations in the 1.4 GHz band, we investigated the relationship between the mass of the central bulge and radio continuum emission in nearby galaxies. Our analysis reveals a positive correlation between the mass of the bulge and the emission of radio continuum, which is influenced by the presence of young stars. We also discovered a connection between the mass of the bulge and the emission of neutral hydrogen. Notably, we found a similar decline in both the radio continuum and neutral hydrogen emissions at high galaxy masses, which may be linked to the suppression of star formation and gas removal. However, we require additional data to confirm this hypothesis. Our research used the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and GMRT-SRT observations and incorporated a bulge-disc decomposition to measure the masses of the bulge and disc components. We defined the mass of the bulge as the sum of the classical and pseudo-bulge components, which are distinct based on their formation histories. We also measured the emission of radio continuum and neutral hydrogen within the central 10 kpc of the galaxies. We controlled for various factors that could influence the radio continuum and neutral hydrogen emissions by employing linear regression analysis. Our results showed a positive correlation between the mass of the bulge and the emission of radio continuum and a similar decline in both the radio continuum and neutral hydrogen emissions at high galaxy masses. We propose that the decrease in both the radio continuum and neutral hydrogen emissions at high galaxy masses may be related to the suppression of star formation and gas removal, although further research is necessary to confirm this hypothesis. X-ray images contain valuable clinical information that can be utilized for predicting patient outcomes.  In this study, we used a convolutional neural network to train a classifier that could indicate whether a COVID-19 patient was critically ill based on their early-stage lung image.  A key aspect of our research involved analyzing the relationship between image features and the patient's critical condition.  To accomplish this, we employed a technique called CAM to visualize the portions of the image associated with predicting severe illness.  Our findings revealed that patients with more severe conditions had specific characteristic features in their images, such as particular patterns in the upper lobe.  By correlating these patterns with the location of virus accumulation in lung tissue, we gained insight into the pathophysiology of severe COVID-19.  Our results showed that larger areas of infected lung tissue were linked to more severe illness but only in patients with lower oxygen levels.  Patients with higher oxygen levels had outcomes determined by different lung infection patterns.  Our study demonstrated that imaging features hold critical value in determining prognosis and that the impact of COVID-19 on the lungs is more complex than previously understood.  Our approach to analyzing the images with a simple neural network allowed us to obtain comparable performance to state-of-the-art techniques while using significantly less data.  Our findings have implications for treating patients with low oxygen levels and suggest that transferring air from healthy parts of the lung may help improve lung function.  Our research also highlights the importance of considering the distribution of infected lung tissue when determining treatment protocols.  Finally, our study demonstrated that features extracted from the images can be used to create 3D models of the infected lung tissue.  Our code is available online for public use. The concept of a simplicial group can be defined using the universal property of simplicial sets, generated by a collection of maps that satisfy specific compatibility conditions. This property enables the construction of a simplicial group from any simplicial set via a universal natural transformation. We demonstrate that the simplicial set associated with a group $G$ serves as the universal starting point for natural transformations to simplicial groups by establishing an isomorphism between the set of natural transformations from $\Delta^{\op}_+\Delta_+G$ and the group $G$ itself. Notably, this result implies that the global simplicial bundle is equivalent to a simplicial group, providing a new interpretation of this concept. Moreover, it allows us to redefine the fundamental group of a simplicial space as the group of natural transformations from the simplicial set to the simplicial circle group, S^1. This definition is beneficial as it yields the correct result when applied to CW-complexes. It also offers a more general framework for extending the concept of fundamental group to simplicial spaces.

Evaluating the truthfulness of breaking news is a critical task that requires immediate attention from the media and the public. False news can spread rapidly, having severe consequences, and accurate verification is essential to prevent this dissemination. Traditional fact-checking methods rely on pre-existing information, which is often inadequate for newly emerging stories. In response, a growing body of research uses machine learning techniques to automatically assess the truthfulness of emerging news. However, training such models for all possible incidents is impractical due to the vast number of events occurring daily. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach, using meta-learning to train a general model that can effectively incorporate information about a specific news item to determine its truthfulness. We evaluate and compare our method to existing approaches using three types of data: text-only, image-only, and multimodal information. The experimental results show that our proposed method excels in both scenarios where model knows about the news item and model does not know about the news item. The code for this research is available in the public domain.

In multi-channel speech processing, improving the quality of individual channels can significantly enhance overall system performance.
We present a novel end-to-end DPCRN network that simultaneously enhances two-channel speech, and experimentally verify its effectiveness for both noisy and multi-microphone scenarios.
By training the network on a single pair of channels, we achieve notable improvements in reverberant environments and outperform state-of-the-art methods when using two channels.
When trained on a single channel, the network excels in noisy conditions and matches the performance of multi-microphone systems in clean environments.
We also explore different training pairs and find that the network performs optimally when using front and rear channels. 
To gain insights into DPCRN's functionality, we substitute the recurrent part with time-domain speech enhancement modules and demonstrate the significance of dual-path structures in addressing non-linear variations. 
Our proposed DPCRN architecture delivers superior results in both individual channel speech enhancement and multi-channel speech separation tasks. 
With proper data augmentation, we achieve a low PER of 5.19\% in the 2i-VAESP task and the DPCRN architecture serves as a solid foundation for future developments in individual channel speech enhancement. 
Our code is available at: \url{https://github.com/EsraaElsawy/DPCRN}.

To simulate atmospheric convection using the multi-fluid model, we've developed a basic approach and conducted a test using a two-fluid version to mimic large-scale atmospheric phenomena. By representing moist air as two distinct fluid components - water vapor and a mixture of other gases - we've created a two-fluid model that effectively mirrors the behavior of moist convection. A single-column model was utilized to simulate a standard dry Rayleigh-Benard convection scenario, both numerically and analytically, serving as a reference to validate our computational method. With slight adjustments to boundary layer conditions, the model accurately replicated the characteristic roll patterns seen in actual convection. Next, we varied the temperature difference between the bottom and top boundaries to observe how it affects roll pattern formation, finding that an odd number of rolls formed when the temperature difference fell within a certain range. These results demonstrate that even a rudimentary multi-fluid model is capable of capturing the intricate features of actual convection rolls. Next, we'll use this model to simulate more complex scenarios, such as cloud-free and cloudy atmospheric conditions. These simulations will help us better understand how the model works and how it can be applied to actual weather patterns. By comparing our simulated results with actual weather data, we'll be able to assess the model's accuracy and identify areas where it needs improvement. Building on these findings, we'll explore more sophisticated multi-fluid model simulations of actual weather patterns. These simulations will help us understand the intricate relationships between clouds, precipitation, and atmospheric convection, paving the way for a more comprehensive, multi-fluid model of the atmosphere. By applying this model to real-world weather scenarios, we'll be able to accurately predict when and where clouds and precipitation will form, thereby enhancing our ability to predict the weather accurately. Ultimately, this research marks the initial step in a broader project aimed at developing a comprehensive, multi-fluid model of the atmosphere, a goal we're confident can be achieved with the help of the international weather research community. To this end, we invite fellow researchers to collaborate with us, offering their expertise and insights to guide the development of this model. By working together, we can create a more advanced, multi-fluid model of the atmosphere that accurately captures the intricate dynamics of clouds, precipitation, and atmospheric convection, a model that will enable us to predict the weather with greater precision and confidence. To facilitate collaboration, we've made the source code of our simulation model publicly available, inviting fellow researchers to use it, modify it, and contribute to its development. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and assessed a range of features and neural network architectures
to determine the most effective method for classifying Twitter posts as positive, negative,
or neutral. Ultimately, we established a baseline using long short-term memory (LSTM) networks
and explored the potential benefits of ensemble methods, resulting in an average of 84% accuracy
over 10-fold cross-validation. Notably, we discovered that employing an LSTM network without
dropout and ensemble techniques achieved 86% accuracy when evaluating sentiment on a held-out
set, surpassing the previous recorded high of 82%. Additionally, we provide a detailed breakdown
of the features' and architectures' performance contributions to the results. By doing so, we hope to
facilitate similar sentiment analysis endeavors on Twitter. The code and data used in this study
are available online.

Quantum states of continuous-variable systems can be described using tomograms, which provide a comprehensive representation of a system's properties. We have developed a method for comparing the entanglement characteristics of continuous-variable states using their tomograms. This approach serves as a starting point for investigating the effects of certain non-gaussian operations that transform tomograms, altering the entanglement measures. Our investigation focuses on three specific operations: amplitude, phase, and beam splitter squeezers. We have analyzed the impact of these squeezers on the tangle and concurrence of two-mode squeezed states. Our results demonstrate that all four squeezers initially increase the tangle and concurrence before entering a saturation phase. We have also examined the synchronization of two independent oscillatory systems using the Wigner function's expectation value of the annihilation operator. This led to a deeper understanding of the relationship between the expectation value of the number operator and the mean of the quadrature operators. Our findings have implications for implementing certain quantum operations that initially increase the tangle and concurrence before entering a saturation phase, which may also enhance the synchronization of oscillatory systems. This is particularly evident in the case of the beam-squeezer, which can be likened to a combination of amplitude and phase squeezers. Notably, all four types of squeezers can produce states with antidotable (i.e., correctable) defects when combined with a two-mode squeezed state. This occurs when the mean of the number operator exceeds a certain threshold, which is dependent on the specific squeezing parameter. This phenomenon can be leveraged to develop a method for identifying and correcting specific types of errors in continuous-variable systems. This is particularly relevant for implementing large-scale continuous-variable systems in the future. The rising popularity of autonomous systems for use in safety-sensitive domains necessitates the development of effective training methods that combine autonomous data collection with human observation. Current approaches, however, are often limited by requiring the expert to continuously observe the system across all tasks, which is impractical given their limited time and resources. In response to this challenge, we introduce a novel learning framework known as Co-Observation Learning without Expert Display (CoLED), which eliminates the need for the expert to observe the system during tasks where it possesses sufficient autonomy. CoLED leverages an observation preference function that prioritizes observation of the system across tasks, with the goal of equally distributing observations across all tasks, thus preventing the system from becoming too reliant on observation in areas where it has mastered sufficient proficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CoLED in reducing reliance on expert observation in areas where the system has gained sufficient autonomy, with notable improvements in both safety and efficiency. With minimal assumptions about the system's underlying behavior, we test CoLED on a range of challenging scenarios, including navigation through complex terrain, where the system requires guidance on 10 to 50% of the terrain, and observe a significant reduction in safety-critical events with minimal initial data requirements. We also compare CoLED to a baseline approach and find it to be significantly more effective in reducing safety-critical events by as much as 72%. We test CoLED on real-world autonomous driving data and find it to be 23% more efficient in reducing safety-critical events. With its ability to distribute observations across tasks, CoLED offers a practical solution for deploying autonomous systems in complex, safety-sensitive domains. We make the code for CoLED available online.

Using reinforcement learning to train neural machine translation models has shown promise, but its efficacy is greatly hampered by the vast number of possible translations.  This issue makes learning extremely difficult, but our proposed solution, ActionDecay, efficiently tackles this problem by dynamically reducing the search space based on the relevance of words to the target sentence.  Our results demonstrate that ActionDecay leads to significant improvements in performance, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods in several benchmarks.  We also find that incorporating a decoder's confidence about the target sentence's fluency further enhances the translated text's quality.  Our approach and data are available open-source on GitHub.  With 16 GP106 GPUs, we achieved outstanding translation speed, attaining 5.4 nucleic sentences per second on the WMT'14 English-to-German benchmark.  Our proposed method ranks 6th among 63 submitted papers to the WMT'19 Test Suite.  Our proposed method's simplicity allows it to be combined with other techniques, and our data reveal that combining ActionDecay with the reinforcement learning technique "Monolingual Backtranslation" leads to significant gains in performance.  Our proposed method can be applied to other machine learning tasks involving large action spaces.  We propose a straightforward approach to evaluate the effectiveness of ActionDecay, and our results demonstrate that ActionDecay efficiently finds the most relevant words within a search space.  We also propose a data-driven method to determine the optimal threshold for discarding infrequent words, and our results demonstrate that ActionDecay's performance varies minimally with different threshold values.  We believe our proposed method and results have implications for other machine learning tasks involving large action spaces. Researchers who drive and dissipate quantum systems at regular intervals often achieve unique non-equilibrium states, which can be more versatile than their equilibrium counterparts. These non-equilibrium states hold great potential for developing robust quantum technology. Quantifying the quantum states and identifying the essential dynamics driving them require highly sensitive measurements. Here, a quantum system consisting of two closely connected, individually driven and dissipated, or "coupled" quantum bits is studied both theoretically and through experimental means using photons, as a key component of a quantum computer building block. By driving the system in a specific way, a steady state is achieved which can be understood using highly precise measurements of the outgoing photons. Contrary to a previous, less accurate model, the discovered description demonstrates that even a very simple, periodic driving method results in a complex, Markov-process-induced state that mimics an alternating pattern of equilibrium states rather than a steady state. This more complex analysis is supported by additional, highly precise measurement data taken at different speeds of data collection. This new description of the state also enables a clearer understanding of the crucial dynamics by mapping the system's parameters onto the quantum state with accurate mathematical calculations. This achievement paves the way for developing similar descriptions for more complex quantum systems based on similar principles. This research was conducted using a superconducting quantum bit system and supported by theoretical explanations using mathematical formulas. The developed description of the quantum state and its dynamics can be replicated in laboratory settings using the following equipment: a superconducting quantum bit system connected to a microwave cavity, a method of driving the system that involves changing the frequency of driving at regular intervals, and a way of measuring the system's parameters that involves calculating the frequency of the outgoing photons based on the cavity's properties. We examine biharmonic hypersurfaces under the Lie derivative in four-dimensional Euclidean space and derive various implications, including whether certain Lie derivative operators lead to hypersurfaces being minimal or having constant mean curvature. We also investigate how these operators interact with each other and with the Yang functional to produce repetitive hypersurfaces with specific symmetry properties. Moreover, we establish conditions under which the Yang functional is constant for hypersurfaces with particular boundary conditions. These findings enrich existing theories and provide a framework for studying biharmonic hypersurfaces that can be applied to a broader class of problems, including some related to the mean curvature flow and minimal surface theories. We conclude by outlining potential applications and suggesting related questions that arise from these discoveries.

Given any real number r greater than 1, we prove the existence of an interval I, whose length is arbitrarily small, and a subset A of the integers within I, such that for any positive irrational number alpha, there is a subinterval of I that contains infinitely many alpha-multiples of lattice points from A and has finite density relative to the interval I. This surpasses a former result by Sarnacchio and Terrani, which only held for a specific, non-arbitrarily small alpha. Additionally, we demonstrate that our initial assumption of r being greater than 1 is not necessary by creating a set A with a specific distribution pattern, which allows for the identification of lattice points from A in any subinterval of (0, 1) with an arbitrarily small length, despite having a finite density within that interval. This in turn enables us to determine the uniqueness of our earlier discovered set A, which is identifiable as (1, q) for any positive integer q. Finally, we examine the connection between our newly defined identifiable sets and those identified by Beresnyei and Terrani, concluding that they are equivalent.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, NoSQL database that has gained popularity in various production environments. Due to its lack of support for transactions across different databases, incorporating MongoDB into existing multi-database transactional systems poses significant challenges. To address this issue, it is essential to examine the concept of transactional integrity in MongoDB, specifically in relation to its document consistency and validation mechanisms. This paper delves into the specifics of MongoDB's document storage, provides a formal framework for defining document consistency, and subsequently develops a method to automate the testing of MongoDB's transactional integrity using existing testing frameworks. By leveraging this approach's ability to simulate various access control mechanisms and test database instances, we successfully validated the transactional integrity of MongoDB with various ACID constraints. Furthermore, we discovered that MongoDB's document validation features can be improved and presented a proposed enhancement to its functionality. This improvement enables MongoDB to efficiently support the majority of existing document-based data management systems within transactional systems. The solar wind, a stream of charged particles flowing from the sun, is influenced by a return current of electrons originating from the planet Earth, known as the solar breeze electron energy flux. This effect is most noticeable during solar minimum when the solar wind is calmer. The innermost region of the solar wind, within 0.25 AU of the sun's surface, has not been studied extensively. A new analysis uses data collected by the Solar Wind Electrons Protons Acceleration Test (SWEPAM) and the Plasma and Energetics Instrument (PEI) on board the Parker Solar Probe to investigate the solar breeze energy flow in the inner heliosphere for the first time. The data cover a 12-month period in 2017 and show that the solar breeze electron energy flux is present and has a similar pattern as observed outside the orbit of Earth, but with a much stronger influence due to the closer distance to the sun and lack of Earth's magnetic field to deflect the electrons. The solar breeze electron energy flow also has a diurnal variation, mirroring that of the interplanetary magnetic field, likely caused by the solar wind's interaction with the solar atmosphere and the resulting field and charge density variations. The analysis reveals an energy flux of approximately 0.1 to 10 nW/m^2, varying based on solar wind speed, density, and the tilt of the sun's surface. The findings suggest that the solar breeze electron energy flow plays a crucial role in powering plasma oscillations in the solar corona and atmosphere, and that it has a significant impact on the solar wind acceleration within the inner heliosphere. The analysis also highlights the importance of considering the energy flux in solar wind models and the need for further research into the solar wind acceleration and the energy balance in the inner heliosphere. Thanks to speech-emotion-recognition-enabled applications such as improved human-computer interaction and enhanced driver behavior, analyzing people's emotions through their speech has become extremely desirable. Nonetheless, developing such systems that can effectively utilize limited data is still a significant challenge. The current state of speech-emotion-recognition systems primarily employs traditional machine learning techniques and rely heavily on vast amounts of training data, which hinders their practical usage. The existing deep learning-based adaptation techniques, although effective for adapting to new domains, fall short in adapting to new tasks with limited data, which impedes the practical implementation of speech-emotion recognition. We present a novel approach that leverages deep reinforcement learning to adapt the system from a simple speech classification task to the complex task of emotion recognition with just a few data samples. The system's ability to effectively utilize limited data enables the creation of practical, real-world-sized systems that can accurately determine people's emotions. When put to use in a scenario where it detects the emotions of drivers, the system demonstrates a notable improvement over the existing methods. The system's efficiency is further proven by conducting additional experiments on the datasets containing multiple classes, which results in comparable or better performance compared to the current deep learning-based techniques. The code for this research has been made available online.

Researchers studying the evolution of over-densities in an increasingly uniform, expanding universe often rely on the "exact" method of matching, expanding with a variable adiabatic index, to analyze perturbations within the Hubble era. However, when considering a much larger over-density with a significant impact, the "exact" method may not be applicable and other approaches, such as the variable adiabatic index method with a quasi-exponential expansion, become more suitable. We examine an extensive over-density characterized by rapid adiabatic expansion and identify the point at which it transitions to an even more expansive, nearly free-falling state. By exploring this transition, we establish the specific over-density threshold required for this free-falling state to develop within an expanding cosmos. Furthermore, we consider a scenario featuring a rapidly expanding void with an empty core and investigate the intense shock wave that forms at the boundary between the void's inner and outer regions. By determining the location of this shock wave, we establish its stability and verify that it remains situated at a fixed distance from the void's core as the cosmos continues to expand. Additionally, we calculate the rate of expansion within the inner region of the void and compare it to the rate of the cosmos' overall expansion. We also examine the influence of varying the adiabatic index and the void's depth, finding that even extreme adjustments have a minimal impact on the shock wave's behavior. By integrating the variable adiabatic index method with a quasi-exponential expansion into an existing model of the multiverse's evolution, we simulate the formation and subsequent expansion of a spherical void, observing how it influences the multiverse's overall structure. We also explore the possibility of a void's existence being indicated by an observed shock wave within our own cosmos. By examining the characteristics of such a shock wave, we are able to deduce its original size, the time at which it formed, and the current rate of the cosmos' overall expansion. We also calculate the distance from us to the point where the void is expanding most rapidly and find that even a void with a depth of 100 megaparsecs would result in a shock wave's formation within our own cosmos, with the void's core located just a few billion light-years away. We also examine the behavior of such a shock wave over time, finding that even if the cosmos were to continue expanding at its current rate, the void would never become completely empty. A striking phenomenon observed in the crackling sound produced by unwinding an adhesive tape appears counter to the conventional understanding of disorder growth. As the tape is unwound, the size of each subsequent loop increases in a disorderly, non-monotonic distribution, yet the sound it makes becomes progressively quieter. To understand this peculiar behavior, we developed a mathematical model that takes into account the changing dimensions of the loops and their potential to produce sound. By analyzing the average size of the loops, we found that the sound the tape makes follows a specific pattern when plotted against the average loop size. This pattern can be explained by a single mathematical equation that captures the underlying dynamics of the disorder growth and sound production. When the average loop size exceeds a certain point, the sound the tape makes becomes significantly quieter, a result that could be relevant to similar systems that exhibit self-similar behavior. This finding can be seen as a manifestation of a broader concept called "confinement-induced order," where the restriction imposed by changing boundaries gives rise to orderly patterns. This idea has been observed previously in other contexts, such as the growth of rivers and mountain ranges, and could provide a more general framework for understanding these systems. To prevent counterparty risk, firms engage in delta hedging with their counterparties, often using options. A crucial aspect in this process is determining the required collateral to compensate for potential losses resulting from changes in stock prices. Prior research has examined this practice, but has generally focused on static scenarios, neglectating time-varying volatility and interest rates. In contrast, this study develops an analytical formula for the expected collateral expenses associated with options in dynamic delta hedging settings, considering variable volatility and interest rates. This formula provides a valuable tool for risk management by taking into account the costs of hedging and the expenses of holding options, and it has been numerically verified to be accurate through comparison with alternative methods. Moreover, it offers a theoretical basis for further generalization to more complex settings. In its current form, the formula can be employed in various numerical methods, such as the finite difference method, by converting it into a closed-form solution for the option payoff. This study also explores the implications of liquidity expenses on option hedging by transforming the option pricing problem into a quasi-variational inequality, but further numerical analysis is required to fully understand these effects. Ultimately, the developed formula and its underlying framework can be used to enhance the efficiency of risk management strategies and option pricing methods in dynamic settings. A dynamic model of social mobility is proposed, where current opportunities influence future social mobility and opportunities in turn are affected by past behavior. The model enables the breakdown of current opportunities into their impact on both immediate and long-term benefits, allowing policy analysis of varied temporal scales of social mobility. Utilizing this dynamic framework, varying levels of opportunity distribution are tested to determine their effect on social mobility in both the short and long term. Results show that increasing opportunity distribution reduces both short-term and long-term inequality but also reveals contrasting findings when examining mobility among different income groups. Ultimately, varying the scope of targeted policies to influence behavior or provide opportunities shows that the latter yields greater benefits in the long run. The model's application to analyzing policy intervention highlights the significance of considering the temporal extent of its impact on social mobility. The proposed dynamic framework can be expanded to incorporate external shocks that affect social mobility over time, enabling a multi-period optimal control approach to find the policy that maximizes long-term social mobility while accounting for present costs. While this broad frequency range offers significant advantages in detecting the signal, it introduces new challenges related to instrumental systematic errors. These errors can arise from signals emitted by instrumental components, such as oscillators, fans, and lighting, which can leak into the detector through feedhorn arrays or other signal paths. The impact of these errors on scientific findings is difficult to assess without simulating the instrumental environment and associated signals.
