Our research introduces a novel approach, utilizing general-purpose document classification models without the need for manual labeling.  We leverage a technique called selective backpropagation to enhance the effectiveness of these models for specific tasks.  To train these models at minimal cost, we employ a pseudo-labeling approach with few initial labeled documents.  Our solution yields significant reductions in labeling expenses: using 100 labeled documents, our method achieves performance comparable to traditional training with 10,000 labeled documents.  Our technique demonstrates versatility by supporting multi-class extractors with a simple modification, and our evaluation framework encompasses multiple evaluation metrics to ensure comprehensive assessment.  Our approach cuts labeling expenses by tenfold while maintaining high performance, an improvement we call the "document reduction factor".  The "document reduction factor" serves as a standardized gauge to compare different approaches' effectiveness in reducing labeling expenses.  Our method excels in multiple application scenarios, with notable improvements in models trained on limited data, models trained on biased data, models combining visual and language cues, and models requiring domain-specific knowledge.  Our research unlocks significant financial savings for companies developing custom extractors for visually intricate documents with limited data and specific requirements. The next generation of gravitational wave detectors will produce a vast number of signals from merging binary compact objects, primarily consisting of binary neutron star, binary black hole, and neutron star-black hole events. However, the overwhelming majority of these events will be weak signals that are detected on a large array of computers used for signal processing. Due to the massive volume of data being captured, real-time analysis through traditional methods on such large scales becomes impractical. A new method, based on deep learning, has been developed to identify these signals on a single computer with a fraction of the memory previously required. This technique utilizes a neural network that is trained to recognize features of the waveforms and accurately classify binary neutron star, binary black hole, and neutron star-black hole events. The network's ability to distinguish between different types of events has been consistently demonstrated across a range of parameters and is found to be highly effective even at low signal-to-noise ratios. Moreover, this model can be trained to recognize specific signals and distinguish them from background noise, thereby enhancing the efficiency of future gravitational wave detection missions. This breakthrough in deep learning applications in gravitational wave analysis has significant implications for the detection of these events in the vast amounts of data captured by the LIGO and Virgo Collaborations. This study analyzed changes in face mask usage and social distancing in urban areas and explored how these changes affected the income-based disparities in these behaviors.  By combining observational data from a public safety camera network in a large North American city, this research employed statistical modeling to explore the spatial patterns of these behaviors and how they changed over time. Specifically, this research found that the income-based disparity in face mask noncompliance in urban areas increased by 45 percent, which may contribute to heightened transmission risks and ultimately worsen income-related health inequities. This research investigates how water waves propagate in the presence of a uniform vertical vorticity forcing a long-crested irregular wave train. We develop a Hamiltonian Hamilton-Dysthe formula that describes how the wave spectrum evolves over time, taking into consideration the effects of uniform vorticity, water depth, shoreline constraints, and a weak dissipation force. We then compare our predicted formula to results obtained through direct numerical simulations of the full water wave problem, finding that the predicted formula accurately predicts the shift in the peak frequency of the wave spectrum and accurately models the occurrence of wave breaking, although it overestimates the rate of change of the wave energy spectrum by a constant factor. We also find that removing the uniform vorticity term in the predicted formula yields a good approximation of the original Hamilton-Dysthe formula, both in its linear and nonlinear forms. We believe that our results have implications for mitigating the effects of uniform vorticity on the evolution of wave spectra, and that they pave the way for further study of more complex scenarios, such as waves in the presence of multiple vortices or rotating water. We conclude by outlining potential research directions for extending our findings in these areas.

For robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar environments, their internal mapping system should ideally incorporate a representation that not only identifies paths but also captures the scene's overall topology. Topological representations are well-suited for this purpose but are typically constructed using place recognition and SLAM methods that rely heavily on visual data and struggle in completely unknown environments. In contrast to conventional approaches, we propose the HiTMap method, which employs a hierarchical layout representation that robot agents can build through exploration without prior knowledge of the environment. HiTMap represents an area as a hierarchical structure composed of connecting corridors and defined areas, without assigning labels to the elements. By focusing solely on navigation, we can circumvent the visual recognition and mapping challenges faced in novel environments. We demonstrate the efficacy of HiTMap in both simulation and real-world experiments, where it efficiently navigates unfamiliar spaces by constructing a clear representation of the layout and distinguishing between different areas. The system's ability to adapt to changing environments without the need for reinitialization also makes it a reliable choice for long-term missions. The code for HiTMap is publicly available online.

By calculating the probability of finding a $\hbar/2$ quantum fluctuation in the superconductor's state, we find that a highly precise atomic interferometry setup can detect even tiny changes in the superconductor's state. This approach can also measure the magnetic interference that surrounds quantum systems and allows for the creation of a "magnetic shield" to protect these systems. This study investigates finite mixture models, a statistical technique used to analyze complex data distributions by breaking them down into simpler components. We show how these models can be connected to geometric methods in probability and the theory of Choquet capacities by utilizing a duality framework. This connection enables us to interpret the parameters of mixture models within geometric probability, specifically using the M\"obius function in relation to Dirichlet measures, and also to bridge them to the theory of Choquet capacities. Leveraging these connections, we can re-express mixture model estimation as an optimization problem in relation to a concave function, facilitating the use of well-established results in convex optimization to solve the estimation problem. We validate our approach through simulations and apply it to real data in genetics. We also discuss the extension of this method to infinite mixture models. The connection to geometric probability and Choquet theory provides new insights into the properties of mixture models, specifically their stability and uniqueness. Allocating memory efficiently on GPUs poses a significant challenge due to their complex memory hierarchy and limited register capacity. Current GPU memory allocators lack support for object-oriented programming techniques that divide code into reusable objects, making it difficult to develop efficient and modular GPU applications. To address this limitation, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator that utilizes small memory blocks to match the limited register capacity of GPUs and features a novel deallocation algorithm to minimize fragmentation and free memory blocks. By combining these features, DynaSOAr enables the use of short-lived objects in GPU applications, leading to a 2.5 times performance improvement and 10 times less memory usage in popular benchmarks and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's efficient memory management enables the development of new GPU applications that leverage object-oriented programming techniques, and it is highly scalable, supporting up to 1024 threads per block with minimal overhead. The DynaSOAr allocator is publicly available for download.

The NASA's TESS mission has made it possible to discover thousands of exoplanets, and this study adds two new discoveries to that list. Using data from the HARPS and TESS observatories, researchers confirmed the existence of two new planets orbiting the star TOI-712. Analyzing the data revealed that the two planets, named b and c, have diameters 30% and 20% larger than Neptune's, respectively. Observations showed that the planets take 4.5 days to orbit the star and have a mass that could indicate they have a significant gas atmosphere. Further analysis revealed that the system may have an additional undiscovered planet, likely a super-Earth, and that the system is young with ages ranging from 45 to 150 million years. This study also found that one of the discovered planets could have a habitable area where temperatures could support liquid water, a requirement for life as we know it. Further observations from HARPS and future missions like the James Webb Space Telescope are needed to better understand the planets' atmospheres and whether the star's solar wind is affecting the inner planet's habitability. This discovery adds to the growing list of exoplanets that could support life and highlights the importance of studying young star systems for similar Earth-like planets. This research was published in the MNRAS journal.

A group G has an algebraic diameter of n if every polynomial equation involving the group's generators and variables has a solution within the group for n-based polynomials. Our research reveals that a finite group with a diameter of n greater than 2-simplex dimension (n > \frac{d(d+3)}{2}-1) inevitably includes a specific type of element known as an n-regular element. In turn, we find that an n-regular element defines the entire group for n less than 4, implying all finite groups with an algebraic diameter of 4 or more are minimal and cannot be defined by lower-order polynomials. Additionally, our approach provides a more in-depth understanding of key concepts, including the relationship between a group's diameter and its capacity to satisfy specific polynomial identities, as well as a characterization of the n-regular elements that comprise the group. Our findings also offer a solution to a conjecture posed by the late mathematician, P.M. Kopp, concerning the finite groups with an algebraic diameter of 4.

A deep infrared survey of the Dragon Nebula, a dark cloud complex, has revealed the presence of 22 young stellar objects (YSOs) within its core region. By correlating the spatial characteristics of polarized light with optical and infrared data, we identified the core region's magnetic field structure, which displays a unique pattern in comparison to the surrounding magnetic field. The core's field is primarily oriented perpendicular to the plane of the sky, which is an uncommon configuration that may indicate the early stages of core formation. However, it's also possible that it's a result of the influence of the large-scale magnetic field. Notably, the core's field configuration differs from that observed in the surrounding molecular cloud, which is more closely tied to the outflowing gas and Larmor radius influenced by the YSOs. By examining the evolutionary stages of the YSOs, we found that the most mature objects are located in the peripheral regions, while the less mature ones are found in the core. This suggests a sequence of evolution from the core to the surrounding cloud, with the most likely outcome being the formation of a massive star. This prediction is supported by the presence of a prominent ridge of dust and gas in the core region, which may eventually give birth to a massive star. This finding is also consistent with simulations showing that massive star formation can originate from a specific type of core with a similar magnetic field configuration. The high concentration of YSOs in the core region and the presence of a massive molecular ridge both contribute to the conclusion that the Dragon Nebula will give birth to a massive star. The discovery of a YSO with an extremely low mass and a large envelope also supports this prediction, as it suggests that the cloud may harbor multiple massive stars. The flow of complex fluids is significantly influenced by surface phenomena due to the high proportion of interface compared to bulk. While the flow of fluids with textured surfaces has been studied extensively, the impact of texture on the surface flow of highly complex liquids, such as liquid foams, is not well understood and is the subject of this study. Using high-speed cameras to observe the flow of liquid foams between two textured plates at varying speeds and distances apart, we have created a theoretical model that accurately explains and predicts observed behavior. By applying the model to a wide range of scenarios, we have identified specific conditions under which increased texture roughness can either increase or decrease friction. Furthermore, we have found that our model aligns with existing theories related to textured surfaces and flow, and has also provided insights into how the configuration of liquid foam lamellae influences friction. By analyzing the configuration of lamellae, we have discovered that the curvature of plate edges can influence the curvature of lamellae curves, leading to a more curved shape in areas further away from the point of plate intersection. This, in turn, contributes to increased friction in these areas. By accounting for this curvature, we have successfully reduced the uncertainty in our model's predictions by a factor of ten. This study highlights the significance of considering the complex internal structure of liquid foams when studying their flow behavior and has implications for the development of models that simulate the flow of similar non-Newtonian liquids. By using a simplified theoretical model, we have also demonstrated that the texture-induced increase in friction in liquid foams can be minimized through the application of a curved surface, thus providing a practical solution that can be implemented in real-world scenarios. Deep learning techniques, particularly Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained significant traction in processing complex and dynamic graph data. As a result, understanding the fundamental workings of GCNNs has become a pressing concern to fully harness their potential. In our study, we delve into the essence of GCNNs by interpreting them through a signal processing lens using matched filtering. This analysis provides valuable insights into the essence of GCNNs, revealing their connection to local signal characteristics and highlighting the significance of spatial signal diversity. We further explore a novel GCNN structure based on the matched filtering framework, which yields a network free of learned representations, thus minimizing the risk of data overfitting. To assess and validate our approach, we develop a comprehensive set of experiments covering both real-world datasets and a synthetic signal diversity scenario. Our findings demonstrate that this new GCNN architecture outperforms existing networks across various tasks and datasets. Our approach offers a unique, data-efficient solution that paves the way for applying GCNNs in dynamic graph environments and provides a precise, quantifiable measure of feature importance that can be used for feature selection and reduction. Our work offers both a starting point for further research and a practical solution for various applications. Our code is available online.

In this paper, we explore a specific gravity theory that combines general relativity and a scalar field, described using Chern-Simons action. This theory results in the emergence of gauge forces in certain situations, such as in the context of AdS (anti-de Sitter space). We are particularly interested in examining the presence of rotating black holes with "hairs" within this framework. However, due to a specific theoretical constraint known as the "hairy ball theorem," we only find solutions where the specific component of angular momentum aligns with the direction of the spacetime curvature. In return, this unique condition allows us to derive a precise expression that links the scalar field to the rate of change in angular momentum. We further investigate a related scenario involving solitons, or stable solitary objects, and discover that the corresponding soliton solutions share an identical expression to the black hole solutions, except with a key difference in the rate of change in angular momentum, which results in solitons being static rather than moving. In both cases, we are able to determine the possible range of the solitons' and black holes' mass by utilizing a specific mathematical property known as the "turning point," which occurs when the gravitational field suddenly changes from being attractive to repulsive. In the process of examining these solutions, we also derive an alternative expression for the AdS space's event horizon using the scalar field, which in return allows us to determine the range of the solitons' and black holes' mass based solely on the characteristics of the scalar field. In the process of analyzing these solutions, we also derive an expression for the gravitational acceleration at the event horizon, which in return enables us to determine the point where the gravitational field becomes too weak to support the solitons' or black holes' mass. Elastography is an advancing medical imaging technique that evaluates the mechanical properties of tissues by measuring the propagation of sound waves. However, accurate elastography relies on precise calculation of lateral displacement data resulting from sound wave interactions with tissues. Current elastography systems face limitations due to insufficient lateral sampling of displacement data caused by insufficient scanning ranges. This research introduces a novel method called Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) to enhance lateral displacement estimation in elastography. By reinterpreting the principles of synthetic aperture imaging, VOSA generates precise and highly sampled estimates of lateral displacement data across any desired scanning range. This approach is tested using numerical models and phantom data, demonstrating improved displacement and strain estimation with reduced scanning ranges. Furthermore, clinical feasibility of VOSA is evaluated using real data from a breast elastography examination, yielding comparable results to conventional methods. While different representations serve various purposes, they often share a common goal of illustrating algorithms and facilitating understanding between individuals. Despite this common objective, there is no established framework to compare and analyze these representations in relation to each other. In contrast to this diverse set of representations, the field of formal programming languages exhibits a unified approach to algorithmic expression, albeit one that is distant from real-world educational demonstrations. To bridge this gap, we propose developing a high-level language we call "rational pseudocode," one that can be used to generate algorithmic demonstrations and, conversely, can be derived from existing educational content to provide a precise, standardized definition of the presented algorithm. A recent breakthrough in multi-agent systems research enables the creation of robust hierarchies by allowing lower-level agents to engage in controlled risk-taking while maintaining overall stability at a higher level. Inspired by this advancement, we investigate a more complex scenario where two autonomous agents navigate a dynamic environment in search of each other, with the pursuer aiming to capture the evader and the evader striving to escape. We introduce a new metric called the pursuer's capture probability as a key performance indicator for guided evolution algorithms. By utilizing capture probability as a fitness function, we can optimize the agents' behavior to meet various safety standards. We further explore different environment configurations to demonstrate the versatility of our approach. One such configuration involves a simple grid environment, whereas another involves a more intricate scenario with moving obstacles. We also examine how the capture probability changes in response to an increase in risk-taking behavior and find that there is an optimal balance between capture and escape scenarios. Furthermore, we discover that the optimal policy exhibits a hierarchical structure when there is a significant distinction in skill levels between the two agents. These breakthroughs lay the groundwork for applying this technology to a broad range of real-world applications, including sports tactics and strategic decision-making in complex environments. We make all code and simulation data available online for further development and experimentation.

Building on the successful model-based method MBMTL, we introduce a new framework, MBMTL-MS, that leverages modular systems to further reduce interference and enable the agent to switch between tasks quickly. By isolating the policy and dynamics networks for each task, the agent can prevent destructive interference and achieve better performance compared to MBMTL. We also explore various system configurations to optimize performance for a wide range of complex scenarios. Our proposed approach can handle an extensive range of tasks, even when they are highly diverse and difficult to switch between. We validate our approach through comprehensive experiments on multiple challenging benchmarks, and it consistently outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods in challenging scenarios. By achieving significant improvements in complex scenarios, we demonstrate the substantial potential of MBMTL-MS for real-world applications. Our approach and underlying methodology are available open-source on GitHub. We also provide detailed guidance for implementing MBMTL-MS in practical settings. These interventions enable us to extract valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of multi-task reinforcement learning. This advancement allows us to effectively monitor and manage interference in practical settings. Through our experiments, we demonstrate that destroying task-specific knowledge can hinder the agent's ability to switch between tasks, while inducing new distinct tasks can make it difficult for the agent to switch between them. Pulsar scintillation, also known as pulse phase smoothness, is a measure that indicates the degree of interference occurring when a pulsar's signal travels through the interstellar medium. By studying the characteristics of this interference, researchers gathered insights about the conditions of the interstellar medium along the path the signal took. These findings were compared to data from a different frequency range, and although there was little difference, both sets revealed similar patterns of variation over time. By modeling these patterns, scientists were able to separate the contributions of the Earth's movement, the pulsar's movement within the galaxy, and the movement of the interstellar medium. The data from the Earth's and pulsar's movements were removed from the patterns of variation, and what remained was used to determine the velocities of the interstellar scintillations''streams' flowing through the galaxy. The average velocity of these streams was found to be around 60 kilometers per second, which is consistent with previous research. In this study, a new end-to-end text-to-speech model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet is proposed, which combines the benefits of pitch-sensitive and raw waveform models to create a more efficient and effective method for generating high-quality speech. By dividing the pitch period into two segments, a periodical model is used to predict periodic components, and a pulse density model is employed to forecast pulse densities for the remaining segments. A pitch-sensitive model then predicts the remaining non-periodic components. Experiments conducted using the LJSpeech dataset yielded a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.25 when using a 12 kHz sampling rate, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art pitch-sensitive WaveNet and source filter model. Moreover, Quasi-Periodic WaveNet demonstrated comparable quality to WaveNet while reducing memory usage by approximately 75%. Additionally, the model exhibited superior generalization capabilities when trained with a shorter duration, achieving a 2.13 MOS when trained with 200 ms utterances compared to 2.07 MOS when trained with 3 s utterances. A 4x reduction in memory usage was also achieved without compromising quality by applying a quantization technique called weight-wise 8-bit floating point. The resulting model, Quantized Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, yielded a 2.23 MOS when using a 12 kHz sampling rate. The open-source code for Quasi-Periodic WaveNet has been made available on GitHub.

Recently, graph neural networks have achieved significant performance in various tasks such as node classification and link prediction. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel GNN architecture that utilizes Lorentzian distances to characterize the relationships between nodes. We are providing an overviews of harmonic gauge choices made in significant gravity theories. Despite the vast literature available on the subject, there's a lack of comprehensive reviews discussing choice of harmonic gauge in General Relativity and its extensions. This note aims to fill this gap by exploring choice of harmonic gauge theories, reviewing choice of harmonic gauge in 3+1 dimensional significant gravity theories, and discussing its implications. We also examine some notable features of specific choice of harmonic gauge, known as harmonic gauge of one-form, and its applications in significant gravity theories. This note's content is intended for researchers and graduate students in theoretical physics who are interested in general relativity and its variations. We hope this note will serve as a foundation for further research and in-depth analysis of choice of harmonic gauge in significant gravity theories. A modified Weyl-Wigner representation is developed to describe and analyze a quantum system in a state of thermal equilibrium. The Weyl-Wigner approach, utilizing a phase space representation, is a powerful tool for examining the spectral properties of a wide range of systems, from non-interacting to many-body and even integrable and chaotic ones. The introduction of a new Weyl-Wigner representation enables a transformation of the Liouville space, which facilitates the derivation of a local thermal equilibrium condition that can be solved analytically. This results in a clear understanding of the conditions under which a local thermal equilibrium is established, and it highlights the significance of rotational symmetry within the context of Weyl-Wigner theory. The proposed framework is specifically applied to examine the local thermal equilibrium behavior of a parametrically coupled bosonic system, and it yields a precise condition for determining the temperature regime within which a local thermal equilibrium is maintained. This is characterized by a specific temperature range, below which the system exhibits both number-fluctuation saturation and a Lorentzian spectral shape. The proposed approach offers a versatile tool for examining local thermal equilibrium behavior in a wide range of systems, from small, closed, and isolated ones to open and semi-autonomous ones. The introduction of a thermal operator that is equivalent to a thermal state operator is also demonstrated, which enables a straightforward derivation of the thermal operator for any local thermal equilibrium state. This is achieved by examining the Liouville space representation of the thermal operator, which results in a non-local operator that is defined in terms of the conormal and normal distributions. The proposed approach is further extended to open systems by introducing a time-dependent thermal operator that is used to derive a generalized collision operator, which enables a straightforward application of the rotating wave approximation. The introduction of a thermal operator also provides a possible alternative to the Bogoliubov approach to the open quantum systems, which can be applied to semi-autonomous and closed systems. The notion of temperature has a positive counterpart in most physical contexts due to the use of a specific distribution function that relies on an exponential term with a negative coefficient involving the Boltzmann constant, kinetic energy, and an affine parameter called temperature. As a result, the absolute temperature scale, introduced by Planck, has a lower bound of 0. Despite its abstract nature, this positive bound has significant implications, influencing various theoretical and practical applications across statistical mechanics, thermodynamics, quantum mechanics, and quantum information, including the central limit theorem, fluctuation-dissipation theorem, Jarzynski equality, Crooks fluctuation theorem, and quantum relative entropy. Given its importance, we have sought an intuitive and geometric explanation for this positive bound, offering a promising future direction for further analysis. Additionally, we have an intriguing discussion on negative absolute temperatures, which have been observed, and we examine the conditions necessary to achieve these temperatures in both non-interacting and interacting systems, concluding with an exploration of their unique properties and potential uses in quantum information applications. This includes the utilization of negative absolute temperatures to create overpopulated states, as well as the implementation of a quantum thermometer protocol. We examine how this framework impacts the behavior of Weakly-Interactive Massive Particles (WIMP) as a potential dark matter component and investigate its influence on the Higgs field's vacuum stability and WIMP's elastic scattering cross-section off nucleons. Furthermore, we establish relationships between the parameters of the scoto-seesaw framework and those of other approaches discussed in the literature. We investigate how relative quantum topological invariants behave when a complex varies, especially in a controlled, or "small", manner. Building on specific cases, we demonstrate how certain localized and modified versions of Chern-Simons and Jones polynomials behave consistently, even when defined over ramified covers. These behaviors are utilized to establish consistency for other related invariants, including colored, twisted versions of these polynomials. Additionally, we explore and generalize these findings to more general, higher-dimensional scenarios, drawing from ideas related to non-commutative birational geometry and the properties of weakly invariant constructions. These properties ensure that certain constructions behave consistently, even when altered in a controlled manner, which in turn ensures the consistency of related invariants when defined over slightly different, closely related objects. These findings provide a framework for generalizing and extending the principles of "additivity" that consistently govern the variations of these invariants, which can be applied to both specific and more general cases. These results and the associated methodologies are also expected to yield valuable insights for a broader, more comprehensive theory of invariants. The safety of radiologists and AI systems can be ensured during radiology tasks by implementing countermeasures to address COVID-19. Although using face masks is common practice, their presence can obscure vital information on patient images, necessitating the development of algorithms to rectify this issue. Here, we propose an innovative method to automatically remove radiologists' face masks from chest X-rays by framing it as an image inpainting task. We employ a combination of U^2-Net and a spatially-adaptive inpainting technique to remove masks from new, unseen data with outstanding results. When evaluating our method on a publicly-available chest X-ray dataset with masks, we find it outperforms existing reference methods according to the PSNR metric by a significant margin of 5.13, demonstrating its superior performance in removing masks from images. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of mask removal on an established chest X-ray disease classification model and discover it has a minimal effect, with an overall accuracy of 94.49% when classifying 13 different diseases with and without removing the masks. With its cutting-edge performance, our method has the potential to be a valuable tool in addressing various illnesses, not just COVID-19. By extending our approach to remove other distracting objects from images, we successfully decrease the false positive rates of the classification model by 7.13% when there are lung lesions present. With its versatility and superior performance, we envision our method being a valuable asset in various clinical settings and emergency situations. Nonlinear dimensionality reduction techniques such as t-SNE have become valuable visualisation tools for specialists working with high-dimensional data. These methods are capable of pinpointing the most significant directions of variation, thereby facilitating the graphical representation of complex data. However, there's a lack of user-friendly tools that make it simple for non-technical individuals to comprehend high-dimensional data and the reduced representations produced by nonlinear dimensionality reduction algorithms. To address this need, ViDaExpert was developed - a free, open-source application designed to help both experts and non-experts navigate and understand high-dimensional data and the corresponding lower-dimensional representations produced by algorithms like t-SNE. ViDaExpert enables users to interactively explore high-dimensional data through various tools, including hyperplane slicing, projection onto lower dimensions, and path tracing. By offering an intuitive interface for non-technical individuals to examine high-dimensional data and the reduced representations produced by nonlinear dimensionality reduction algorithms, ViDaExpert provides a valuable resource for fields such as biology, medicine, and social sciences that frequently employ such analyses. The application source code is available on GitHub under the Apache License v2.0. The ViDaExpert user interface is available to try online.
